findings.title: Normalization precedes the relative-path '/' prefix in RedirectRule
findings.body:
RedirectRule later prepends '/' when `newPath[0] != '/'` (the no-scheme branch). The collapse runs before that step, so a replacement result such as `\\evil.com` becomes `/\\evil.com`, which is still scheme-relative. The same applies to any value starting with '\\'.

Suggestion: Apply CollapseLeadingSlashes after the '/' prefix is added, or extend the normalizer to treat a leading '\\' as a slash, e.g. check `url[0] is '/' or '\\'`.
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Collapse runs before '/' is prepended, so backslash-led targets bypass it
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Rewrite path collapse has the same ordering gap
findings.body:
The path branch below this line prepends '/' when the path does not start with '/'. A pattern starting with '\\' therefore still becomes `/\\host` in Request.Path, which defeats the stated defense-in-depth goal.

Suggestion: Normalize after the leading '/' has been added to the path component.
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Normalizer ignores a leading backslash
findings.body:
The early return requires `url[0] == '/'`. Inputs that begin with '\\' (for example `\\/evil.com` or `\\\\evil.com`) are returned untouched. Every caller then prepends '/' to such values, so the helper does not actually provide the guarantee its comment claims, and it does not mirror IsLocalUrl.

Suggestion: Treat both separators at index 0: `if (url.Length == 0 || (url[0] != '/' && url[0] != '\\')) return url;`, then scan the leading run starting at index 0.
findings.label: defect:d1

findings.title: Backslash request-path cases likely don't exercise backslashes
findings.body:
System.Uri converts '\\' to '/' in http(s) paths. The request `legacy/\\example.com` is therefore sent as `legacy//example.com`, and these cases duplicate the `//` case. The same applies to the backslash InlineData in the ModRewrite and IIS tests. No test covers a target that begins with '\\', which is exactly the case the implementation misses.

Suggestion: Use a percent-encoded backslash (`%5C`) in request paths, and add cases where the replacement or back-reference yields a leading '\\' (e.g. replacement `\\\\example.com` or `$1` with a `%5Cexample.com` capture).
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Normalize after the '/' prefix is added, not before
findings.body:
`CollapseLeadingSlashes` runs before the branch that prepends '/' to targets lacking a scheme or a leading slash.

Take an IIS rule `url="{R:1}"` where the capture is `\/evil.com` or `\evil.com`:
1. The helper returns it unchanged, because it only acts when `url[0] == '/'`.
2. The next line turns it into `/\/evil.com` or `/\evil.com`.
3. Browsers resolve that as a scheme-relative URL to evil.com.

The open redirect the change is meant to close is therefore still reachable through RedirectAction.

Suggestion: Move `pattern = UrlNormalizer.CollapseLeadingSlashes(pattern);` to after the `if (... pattern[0] != '/') pattern = '/' + pattern;` block, or have the helper itself handle a leading '\'.
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Helper misses leading backslash and whitespace/control-char variants
findings.body:
The early-return guard requires `url[0] == '/'`, so these inputs pass through untouched:
- `\\evil.com`
- `\/evil.com`

WHATWG URL parsers treat both as scheme-relative. In RedirectRule a replacement like `$1` with such a capture is emitted as-is.

The loop also stops at tab, CR or LF. Browsers strip those characters before parsing, so `/\t/evil.com` still resolves to evil.com.

The comment says the helper mirrors `IsLocalUrl`, but its coverage is narrower than a sound check.

Suggestion: Treat both '/' and '\\' as slash characters starting at index 0, and skip ASCII tab/CR/LF inside the leading run, e.g. `while (i < url.Length && (url[i] is '/' or '\\' or '\t' or '\r' or '\n')) i++;` then return `"/" + rest` whenever the run contains at least two slash characters.
findings.label: defect:d1

findings.title: Breaks intentionally configured scheme-relative redirects
findings.body:
The collapse is applied to the whole result of `Replacement`, including literal text written by the administrator. An existing rule such as `AddRedirect("(.*)", "//cdn.example.com/$1")` used to redirect off-host and now silently redirects to the local path `/cdn.example.com/...`. The new test `CheckRedirect_CollapsesSchemeRelativeTarget` with replacement `//example.com` asserts this new behavior.

This is a silent breaking change with no opt-out and no diagnostic.

Suggestion: Only sanitize when the leading slashes come from substituted request data. Alternatively, document this as a breaking change and offer an opt-out or a logged warning when a configured literal replacement begins with '//'.
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Same ordering gap if RewriteAction later prefixes '/'
findings.body:
Normalization happens before the downstream code that splits the path and query and prepends '/' to relative paths. A rewritten value that starts with '\' therefore ends up in Request.Path as `/\...` without being collapsed. This defeats the stated defense-in-depth goal for downstream redirects.

Suggestion: Apply the normalization to the final path string assigned to `Request.Path`, i.e. after any '/' prefixing.

findings.title: Backslash-led back-reference still yields scheme-relative Location
findings.body:
RedirectRule matches against the request path with its leading '/' stripped. With `AddRedirect("(.*)", "$1")`, a request to `/\evil.com` gives `newPath = "\evil.com"`. `CollapseLeadingSlashes` returns that unchanged because the first character is not '/'. The later `newPath[0] != '/'` branch then prepends '/', producing `/\evil.com`, which browsers resolve to `//evil.com`. The fix is bypassed for the most common redirect pattern.

Suggestion: Apply the normalization after the code that prepends '/', or extend UrlNormalizer to collapse any leading run of '/' and '\' whether or not the first character is '/'.

findings.label: valid

findings.title: Do not silently rewrite developer-configured scheme-relative redirects
findings.body:
The normalization runs on the final target, not only on the part captured from the request. A replacement written deliberately as `//cdn.example.com/path` (a protocol-relative redirect to another host) now sends users to `/cdn.example.com/path` on the same site. The new test on lines 178-181 of MiddlewareTests.cs asserts exactly this.

Rewrite ships in the shared framework, where breaking behavior changes are highly discouraged. A default-on behavior change in servicing must provide an opt-out, and this change has none. RedirectAction and RewriteAction have the same problem.

Suggestion: Limit the normalization to the substituted back-reference values, so attacker-controlled input is sanitized but literal configuration is left alone. Otherwise, gate it behind an opt-out switch such as an AppContext switch, and document the behavior change.
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Internal rewrite paths are altered without a redirect being involved
findings.body:
RewriteAction only assigns the result to Request.Path, which is server-internal. Collapsing `//` and `\` here changes routing for apps that rely on rewritten paths containing those sequences, for example rules that pass through a captured segment. It does not close any vulnerability in this component. The 'downstream may redirect' reasoning would equally apply to the original incoming Request.Path, which is not normalized. This adds behavior drift for little security gain.

Suggestion: Drop the normalization from RewriteAction. If it must stay, keep it behind the same opt-out as the redirect change.
findings.label: nit

findings.title: Normalization bypass
findings.body:
`CollapseLeadingSlashes` runs before the code that prepends `/` to relative patterns, and it only acts when the string already starts with `/`. A pattern that starts with a backslash skips normalization, then gets `/` prepended, which recreates the scheme-relative shape.

Example: the IIS rule `url="{R:1}"` with a capture of `\example.com` (or `\\example.com`) becomes `/\example.com`. Browsers treat that as `//example.com`, so the open redirect still works. The same applies to Apache rules like `RewriteRule /legacy/(.*) $1 [R=302]`.

Fix: normalize after the leading `/` is prepended, or make the helper also collapse a leading run that begins with `\`. Add test cases where the target has no leading `/` and the capture starts with `\`.
findings.label: valid

notes: Open redirect: the new mitigation is incomplete for `RedirectAction`. A back-reference that starts with `\` passes through `CollapseLeadingSlashes` unchanged, then has `/` prepended. This produces a `Location` such as `/\evil.com`, which browsers resolve off-origin when `PathBase` is empty.

findings.title: Open redirect bypass
findings.body:
`CollapseLeadingSlashes` runs before the code that prepends `/` to relative patterns, so the result of that prepend is never normalized.

Concrete case:

- The helper returns it unchanged, because `url[0] != '/'`.

- Browsers treat `/\example.com` as scheme-relative, so the redirect is still open.

A rewrite sets Request.Path and emits no Location header, so no open redirect arises here. The comment itself says this is speculative defense in depth. The collapse changes the path seen by downstream middleware, so a rewrite to a path with a legitimate leading `//` or `/\` (for example a proxied or catch-all route) is silently altered. findings.title: Deferred update flag leaks if popup opening throws
findings.body:
`_isOpeningOverflowPopup` is reset in `finally`, but `ApplyDeferredDynamicOverflowUpdate()` runs only on the success path. Suppose `_overflowPopup.IsOpen = true` throws after an update was deferred. `_hasDeferredDynamicOverflowUpdate` then stays true, and the overflow layout stays stale until some later open happens to flush it. Other `RequestDynamicOverflowUpdate` calls run `UpdateDynamicOverflow` directly but never clear the flag, so a spurious extra recompute happens on the next open.

Suggestion: Clear `_hasDeferredDynamicOverflowUpdate` inside `UpdateDynamicOverflow`, or call `ApplyDeferredDynamicOverflowUpdate()` from the `finally` block after resetting the opening flag.
findings.label: nit

findings.title: Re-entrancy guard only covers the synchronous IsOpen setter
findings.body:
The original crash comes from mutating `_overflowItems` while the overflow ItemsControl is realizing containers. The guard is active only for the duration of `_overflowPopup.IsOpen = true`. Realization can also happen outside that window, during a later layout pass, a re-measure while the popup is open, or a template re-application. In those cases a visibility change raised during container realization still calls `UpdateDynamicOverflow` re-entrantly. That clears and refills the collection being enumerated, so the crash is fixed only for the specific path the test exercises.

Suggestion: Guard on the actual mutation, e.g. set a flag while `UpdateDynamicOverflow` or overflow-presenter realization is running. Alternatively, coalesce requests via `Dispatcher.UIThread.Post` when a request arrives while the overflow presenter is realizing or arranging.
findings.label: invalid

findings.title: Test does not close window and under-asserts the deferred update
findings.body:
The created `window` is never closed, which can leak state into other tests in the same scope. The test checks only that no exception occurred and that `IsVisible` is false. It never verifies that the deferred `UpdateDynamicOverflow` actually ran, for example that the hidden secondary command is no longer counted, or that overflow button visibility and the separator state reflect the change.

Suggestion: Wrap the test in try/finally with `window.Close()`. Add an assertion on `cb.OverflowItems` or the overflow presenter contents after opening.
findings.label: nit

findings.title: Guard the popup close path against re-entrant overflow updates
findings.body:
Only the open path sets `_isOpeningOverflowPopup`. The `else` branch, which sets `_overflowPopup.IsOpen = false`, still lets visibility subscriptions, size changes and measure passes call `UpdateDynamicOverflow` synchronously. Closing the popup detaches and unrealizes overflow items. A secondary command that toggles `IsVisible` on detach can therefore still trigger an overflow-collection mutation in the middle of a presenter update. That is the same class of re-entrancy this change fixes for opening.

Suggestion: Generalize the guard to `_isTogglingOverflowPopup`. Wrap both `IsOpen = true` and `IsOpen = false` with it, and call `ApplyDeferredDynamicOverflowUpdate()` after each.
findings.label: invalid

findings.title: Make the regression test exercise the overflow-realization path
findings.body:
`VisibilityChangingCommandBarButton` hides itself the first time `Parent` becomes non-null. If `CommandBar` adds `SecondaryCommands` to its logical children, or the window attaches them, `Parent` is already set before `cb.IsOpen = true`. The visibility change then happens outside the popup-opening window, so the test passes with or without the fix. The test also never checks that the deferred update ran: it does not assert overflow button visibility, separator state, or overflow item contents after open.

Suggestion: Trigger the visibility change from something that only happens during overflow realization, such as `OnAttachedToVisualTree` while `IsOpen` is true or the overflow presenter's container-prepared hook. Then assert the post-update overflow state, for example that the overflow button is hidden or the overflow presenter is empty.

findings.title: Suppressing reposition disables screen-edge constraint for growing pointer popups
findings.body:
Once `_hasInitialPosition` is true, every size-driven reposition is dropped for `PlacementMode.Pointer`. That repositioning is also what re-runs the positioner's constraint adjustment (flip/slide).

A context flyout opened near the bottom or right edge whose content grows later will extend off-screen and get clipped. Examples are async-loaded items, expanding submenus and text changes. Before this change it was shifted back into view.

The fix trades a jump-on-resize bug for an off-screen bug.

Suggestion: Keep the anchor point fixed but still allow constraint adjustment. For example, reposition only when the new bounds would exceed the screen work area, or re-run the positioner using the original anchor rect and the new size instead of skipping it entirely.

findings.title: End-anchor heuristic fires whenever viewport equals panel bounds, not only when scrolled to end
findings.body:
The new early return treats `viewportEnd >= Bounds.Height` (or `Width`) as 'scrolled to the end' and jumps the anchor to `itemCount - 1`. That only holds when the panel is larger than the viewport and the user has scrolled to the bottom.

It breaks in these cases:

- In all of those, the effective viewport equals the panel bounds, so the condition is true on every measure where `_hasReachedEnd` is false.
- Example: a horizontal VSP with 1000 items whose realized items do not reach the last one. On the next measure it skips the realized-element anchor and re-anchors at the last item. The panel then shows the tail of the list instead of the head.

`Bounds` is also the size from the previous arrange. It is (0,0) before the first arrange and stale after collection or estimate changes, which makes the comparison unreliable.

This path also bypasses the existing realized-elements anchor logic entirely, so it overrides normal incremental scrolling whenever it triggers.

Suggestion: Base the decision on actual scroll state rather than the panel's own Bounds. For example, only take this path when the viewport offset in the U direction is non-zero and `viewportEnd` is close to the previously reported extent. Alternatively, handle it as an explicit 'scroll to end' request coming from the ScrollViewer. At minimum, require `_viewport.Top/Left > 0` and `Bounds` to be non-empty.

The controller also takes a `DbConnection` and builds its own `DbCommand`. ADR-0001 forbids both: move this query into `OrderRepository` and pass `customerPrefix + "%"` as a `DbParameter`. Separately, `TotalFor` dereferences the result of `FirstOrDefault` without a null check. An unknown `orderId` throws `NullReferenceException`.
findings.label: defect:sqli

findings.title: Race / async void
findings.body:
`Parallel.ForEach` does an unsynchronized read-modify-write on a shared static `Dictionary`. Concurrent rows can lose totals or corrupt the dictionary's internal state.

`ImportAsync` is `async void`, which ADR-0002 forbids. Callers cannot await it, and exceptions will crash the process. This includes the parse errors and `IndexOutOfRangeException` that malformed rows will throw.

`StreamReader` is never disposed.

Each non-USD row calls `RateService.ToUsd`, which creates a `new HttpClient()` and blocks on `.Result`. This can exhaust sockets and thread-pool threads under parallel load, and also violates ADR-0002.
findings.label: defect:race

findings.title: Off-by-one
findings.body: The loop condition `i <= start + size` returns `size + 1` items. For example, `Window(items, 0, 10)` returns 11 elements. It should be `i < start + size`. A negative `start` also throws `ArgumentOutOfRangeException` from the indexer, and it is not validated the way `Page` validates its arguments.
findings.label: defect:offbyone

notes: SQL injection: `OrdersController.CountMatching` builds SQL by concatenating user input into a `LIKE` clause. An attacker can read or alter arbitrary data.

Sensitive information exposure: `src/Data/Db.cs` hardcodes the production connection string, including the password (`Sh0p!Prod#2026`), in source. This violates ADR-0001. The credential should be rotated and loaded from configuration or the environment instead.

Insecure password reset token: `PasswordHasher.ResetToken` is an unkeyed MD5 of the email plus the current date. Anyone who knows a user's email can compute a valid token and take over the account. Generate tokens with `RandomNumberGenerator`, store them server-side (preferably hashed), and give them an expiry.
Minor: `RateService` interpolates `currency` from the CSV into the URL without encoding, which allows query-parameter injection.

findings.title: Eliminate SQL injection via repository parameterization
findings.body:
Concatenating `customerPrefix` into `CommandText` is a SQL injection vulnerability. It also breaks ADR-0001, which forbids controllers from using `DbConnection` and requires every `LIKE` pattern to be passed as a `DbParameter`. Move the query into `OrderRepository` and pass `customerPrefix + "%"` as a parameter value. Then remove `DbConnection` from the controller constructor.

Improved code:
public Task<int> CountMatching(string customerPrefix, CancellationToken ct) =>
    orders.CountByCustomerPrefixAsync(customerPrefix, ct);
findings.label: defect:sqli

findings.title: Remove hardcoded production database credentials
findings.body:
This commits a production database password to source control. ADR-0001 requires connection strings to come from configuration or the environment. Load the value from `IConfiguration`, and rotate the exposed `shop_app` password because it is now in git history.

Improved code:
public static string ConnectionString(Microsoft.Extensions.Configuration.IConfiguration config) =>
    config.GetConnectionString("Shop")
        ?? throw new InvalidOperationException("Connection string 'Shop' is not configured.");

findings.title: Non-thread-safe Dictionary mutated inside Parallel.ForEach
findings.body:
Multiple threads read and write the static Dictionary without synchronization. The read-modify-write at line 22 loses updates even on a safe collection. Concurrent writes to Dictionary can corrupt its internal state, causing exceptions or infinite loops. The static state is also shared across imports and read concurrently by TotalFor. Each row also makes a blocking HTTP call through ToUsd, and the loop has no handling for short rows (cols[3] throws IndexOutOfRange) or unparseable numbers.

Suggestion: Use ConcurrentDictionary with AddOrUpdate, or aggregate per-thread and merge. Cache rates per currency before the loop. Validate cols.Length and use decimal.TryParse with InvariantCulture.
findings.label: defect:race

findings.title: New HttpClient per call, blocking .Result, no caching or timeout
findings.body:
Creating an HttpClient per call (and never disposing it) exhausts sockets and defeats connection reuse. `.Result` blocks a thread and can deadlock under a synchronization context. In the import it runs once per row from parallel threads, which hammers the external API. The currency value is interpolated into the URL without escaping, and there is no timeout, status check or error handling.

Suggestion: Use a shared or injected HttpClient (IHttpClientFactory), make the method async (`await client.GetStringAsync(...)`), cache rates per currency, and use Uri.EscapeDataString(currency).
findings.label: defect:dispose

findings.title: Off-by-one: Window returns size + 1 items
findings.body:
The loop condition `i <= start + size` includes index start + size, so up to size + 1 elements are returned, contradicting the capacity and the sibling Page method. A negative start also throws ArgumentOutOfRangeException on items[i], and start + size can overflow.

Suggestion: for (var i = Math.Max(start, 0); i < items.Count && result.Count < size; i++)
findings.label: defect:offbyone

findings.title: SQL injection via string-concatenated LIKE clause
findings.body:
`customerPrefix` is concatenated directly into the SQL text. An attacker can inject arbitrary SQL, for example `x' OR 1=1 --` or a UNION/stacked query, which can leak or modify data. LIKE wildcards (`%`, `_`) in the input are also not escaped.

Suggestion: var p = cmd.CreateParameter(); p.ParameterName = "@prefix"; p.Value = customerPrefix + "%"; cmd.Parameters.Add(p); cmd.CommandText = "SELECT COUNT(*) FROM orders WHERE customer LIKE @prefix";
findings.label: defect:sqli

findings.title: Production database credentials hardcoded in source
findings.body:
The connection string contains the production host, user and password, and it is committed to source control. Anyone with repo access, or any leaked build artifact, exposes the production database. The password must be treated as compromised. `TrustServerCertificate=True` also disables TLS certificate validation, which allows man-in-the-middle attacks.

Suggestion: Rotate the password. Load the connection string from configuration or a secret store (environment variable, Key Vault), and remove TrustServerCertificate.
findings.label: defect:secret

findings.title: Unsynchronized Dictionary mutated from Parallel.ForEach
findings.body:
`TotalsByCustomer` is a plain static `Dictionary` that is read-modify-written from multiple threads. This causes lost updates, corrupted internal state, exceptions, or infinite loops during resize. The read-then-write is also not atomic, so totals are wrong even without corruption. The parallel body also makes a blocking HTTP call per row via `rates.ToUsd`.

Suggestion: Use a ConcurrentDictionary with `AddOrUpdate`, or aggregate per thread and merge. Fetch rates once per currency before the loop.
findings.label: defect:race

findings.title: Predictable password reset token (MD5 of email + date)
findings.body:
The token is an unkeyed MD5 of the email and the current date. Neither is secret, so anyone who knows a user's email can compute a valid token for today and take over the account. The token is not random, not single-use, and not bound to a stored expiry. It also becomes invalid at UTC midnight, which breaks legitimate users.

Suggestion: Generate a random token with `RandomNumberGenerator.GetBytes(32)`. Store only its hash with an expiry and a single-use flag, and compare in constant time.
findings.label: defect:md5

findings.title: FirstOrDefault result dereferenced without a null or default check
findings.body:
If no order matches `orderId`, `FirstOrDefault` returns null (for a class) and `order.Total` throws NullReferenceException. If `Order` is a struct, it silently returns a default total of 0, which is misleading.

Suggestion: var order = found.FirstOrDefault(o => o.Id == orderId) ?? throw new KeyNotFoundException(...); or return a nullable result.

findings.title: async void method and undisposed StreamReader
findings.body:
`async void` means callers cannot await completion or observe exceptions. A parse error crashes the process via the synchronization context or thread pool. The `StreamReader` is never disposed, so the file handle leaks. Rows are parsed with no bounds checks, so a short row throws IndexOutOfRange, and naive `Split(',')` breaks on quoted fields.

Suggestion: public async Task ImportAsync(string csvPath, CancellationToken ct = default) { using var reader = new StreamReader(csvPath); ... }

Creating an `HttpClient` per call without disposing it exhausts sockets under load. `.Result` blocks the thread and can deadlock or starve the thread pool, and here it is called inside `Parallel.ForEach` for every non-USD row. findings.title: Password reset token is predictable (MD5 of email + date)

The token is an unsalted, unkeyed MD5 of the email and today's date. Both inputs are known or guessable, so an attacker can compute any user's valid reset token and take over the account. findings.title: Overflow Bypasses Cap
findings.body: `1 << attempt` overflows for large attempt counts, so the `d > 30` cap never applies. On 64-bit platforms, `attempt` = 63 yields a negative value and `attempt` >= 64 yields 0. A long-running retry loop that keeps incrementing `attempt` would then wait zero or a negative duration and spin without backoff. A negative `attempt` panics at runtime. Clamp `attempt` before shifting, for example by returning 30 when `attempt >= 5` and treating `attempt < 0` as 0.
findings.label: nit

findings.title: Unit Contract Change
findings.body: The exported `Delay` used to return milliseconds (`100 << attempt`) and now returns seconds (1 to 30). Existing callers that convert the result with `time.Millisecond` would silently get 1–30 ms waits instead of 100 ms or more. Callers that switch to seconds would get very different timings. The callers are not in this diff, so verify that every call site was updated for the new unit, or rename the function or return a `time.Duration` so the change can't be missed.

findings.title: Overflow Bypasses Cap
findings.body: `1 << attempt` overflows for large attempt counts, so the `d > 30` cap never applies. On 64-bit platforms, `attempt` = 63 yields a negative value and `attempt` >= 64 yields 0. A long-running retry loop that keeps incrementing `attempt` would then wait zero or a negative duration and spin without backoff. A negative `attempt` panics at runtime. Clamp `attempt` before shifting, for example by returning 30 when `attempt >= 5` and treating `attempt < 0` as 0.

findings.title: File handle from cache.Load is never closed
findings.body:
cache.Load returns a Handle that keeps the opened *os.File open (it only closes it on a read error). Summary reads the bytes and returns without releasing the handle, so each call leaks a file descriptor. A server that calls Summary repeatedly will eventually hit the fd limit and every later open will fail.

Suggestion: Close the handle after use, e.g. `defer h.Close()` if Handle exposes Close. Otherwise change cache.Load to close the file after ReadAll, since the data is already fully buffered.

findings.body:
Delay used to return milliseconds (100<<attempt) and now returns seconds (1<<attempt). Callers that treat the value as milliseconds, such as time.Duration(Delay(n))*time.Millisecond, will now wait 100x less (1 ms instead of 100 ms for attempt 0). The signature is unchanged, so the compiler cannot flag it. The base delay also changed, from 100 to 1 unit. Callers that treat it as seconds would see a very different wait, and the cap of 30 is now low relative to the old values.

Suggestion: Return a time.Duration so the unit is explicit, or rename the function, and update every caller.

findings.title: ID-0 fallback skipped whenever a specific entry exists
findings.body:
The ID-0 lookup only runs when both `policy` and `agg_policy` are NULL. Once `aggregate_for_identity` returns a non-zero aggregate, any map entry keyed on ID 0 is ignored if a specific-ID entry matched.

This matters if the entry was inserted by a path other than `L4Filter.toMapState`, such as a wildcard deny or a higher-precedence/longer-prefix L4-only entry. The lower-precedence specific entry would then win, and a deny could be bypassed.

The new expansion only covers `toMapState`'s wildcard case. So either every ID-0 producer must be expanded to all aggregates, or the datapath must always consider ID 0 in the precedence comparison.

Suggestion: Either always include the ID-0 entry in the precedence comparison, or guarantee and assert in userspace that no ID-0 keys are ever written once aggregates differ from 0, and drop the fallback.

findings.title: Exported mutable var defines datapath contract

`AllAggregates` is an exported, mutable package variable. It must stay in lockstep with `aggregateFor` and with the BPF `aggregate_for_identity`. Any package can mutate it at runtime.

Nothing ties the three definitions together, such as a test that checks every `aggregateFor(x)` result is in `AllAggregates`. Drift would cause wildcard policy to be keyed on IDs the datapath never looks up.

Suggestion: Unexport the variable or expose it via a function. Add a unit test asserting consistency between `aggregateFor` and the aggregate list.

Any downstream code that appends to, sorts or modifies `idents` in place would silently corrupt the global wildcard list for every later policy computation. That would be very hard to debug.

Suggestion: Return a copy, e.g. `idents = slices.Clone(AllAggregates)`, or make `AllAggregates` unexported and accessed through a function that returns a fresh slice.

findings.title: Aggregate-key detection only works for identity 0
findings.body:
The iterators compute `agg := aggregateFor(key.Identity)` and treat the key as an aggregate key when `key.Identity == agg`. By the `aggregates()` contract (`agg != child && aggregateFor(child) == agg`), an aggregate is not its own aggregate. So for any future non-zero aggregate X, `aggregateFor(X)` returns X's parent (e.g. 0), never X, and the comparison is false. The same pattern appears in BroaderOrEqualKeys (280), CoveredNarrowerOrEqualKeys (303), NarrowerOrEqualKeys (337/349) and lookup (437/443). When X is passed, its covered children are never iterated, and `lookup`/insert treat X as a specific ID. This silently breaks the coverage invariants these functions are being generalized to support, and it will not show up as a compile or test failure while `aggregateFor` returns 0.

Suggestion: Introduce an explicit predicate such as `isAggregate(id)` and use it to choose the branch. For an aggregate key, use `key.Identity` itself as the `agg` argument to `forCoveredIDs`. For example: `if isAggregate(key.Identity) { ms.forCoveredIDs(key.Identity, k, idSet, yield) }`, and use `aggregateFor` only to find the parent aggregate of a specific key.

findings.title: Wildcard (ID 0) entries ignored when the aggregate is non-zero
findings.body:
`CoveringBroaderOrEqualKeys`, `BroaderOrEqualKeys` and `LPMAncestors` now visit only `key.Identity` and `aggregateFor(key.Identity)`. Previously ID 0 was always visited, because ANY covers every identity.

If `aggregateFor(X)` returns a non-zero aggregate A for some X, entries keyed on identity 0 are never yielded as covering X. The same applies to `lookup` (lines 429-449). Consequences:
- A broad deny or higher-precedence entry with ANY identity would not be seen as covering X's entries.
- Insertion and coverage pruning could keep entries that should have been suppressed, or miss deny precedence.
- `lookup` would return a verdict that ignores L4-only (ID 0) rules.

This holds unless the datapath equally ignores ID 0 for such identities, or aggregation is guaranteed to always be 0.

Suggestion: Walk the full aggregation chain (X -> A -> ... -> 0) when collecting covering keys. Alternatively, document and assert that every non-zero aggregate is itself the only covering wildcard for its members, and that ID-0 entries can never apply to them.
findings.label: nit

findings.title: ID-0 fallback only runs when no specific entry matched
findings.body:
The ID-0 fallback runs only when both lookups missed (`!agg_policy && !policy`). It is skipped in two cases:
- A specific-ID entry was found but has lower precedence.
- `remote_id` is itself an aggregate, which skips the aggregate lookup.

If an ID-0 deny (or higher-precedence proxy) entry exists without being expanded into the aggregate, a lower-precedence specific allow wins and the wildcard deny is silently bypassed.

The fallback therefore cannot be relied on for precedence-correctness, and is redundant if userspace always expands ID 0 to every aggregate. Today `aggregate_for_identity` returns 0, so this is latent. It becomes a policy-bypass bug as soon as non-zero aggregates are introduced.

Suggestion: Pick one model. Either guarantee that userspace never emits ID-0 entries once aggregates exist, and remove the fallback. Or run the ID-0 lookup whenever the aggregate is non-zero and include it in the precedence comparison.

findings.title: "Is aggregate key" test contradicts the aggregateFor/aggregates contract
findings.body:
The iterators decide that a key is an aggregate key with `key.Identity == aggregateFor(key.Identity)`. That only holds if `aggregateFor` maps an aggregate to itself, which today is true only for 0. Meanwhile `aggregates(agg, child)` requires `aggregateFor(child) == agg && agg != child`, i.e. `aggregateFor` maps a child to its parent.

Once `aggregateFor` returns a real non-zero aggregate A for children, an aggregate key A has `aggregateFor(A) != A`. It would then be treated as a specific identity: its children would never be visited, and `forCoveredIDs` would be called with the wrong parent.

The broader-key iterators would also stop visiting identity 0 (the true wildcard), because they only check one level, `agg`. This affects `CoveringBroaderOrEqualKeys`, `BroaderOrEqualKeys` and `LPMAncestors`. Wildcard entries would then be silently ignored when computing coverage and precedence.

Suggestion: Add an explicit `isAggregate(id)` predicate rather than relying on `id == aggregateFor(id)`. Make the ancestor iterators walk the full aggregate chain (id → aggregateFor(id) → … → 0), or document and assert that aggregation is single-level with 0 as the only aggregate.

findings.title: Aggregate-key detection only works for identity 0

The iterators decide whether the supplied key is an aggregate by checking `key.Identity == aggregateFor(key.Identity)`, i.e. whether the key is its own aggregate. That only holds for `IdentityUnknown`. Once `aggregateFor` returns real non-zero aggregates, an aggregate key A would get `aggregateFor(A)` equal to A's parent, not A. As a result:
- `BroaderOrEqualKeys`, `CoveredNarrowerOrEqualKeys` and `NarrowerOrEqualKeys` would skip the covered child identities.
- `forCoveredIDs` would be passed the wrong aggregate.

The abstraction looks general but silently produces wrong iteration results as soon as it is used for its stated purpose. The same pattern appears at lines 296/303 and 330/337.

Suggestion: Determine aggregate-ness from the key itself, e.g. `isAggregate(key.Identity)`, and pass `key.Identity` as the aggregate to `forCoveredIDs` for aggregate keys. Use `aggregateFor(key.Identity)` only to find the covering aggregate of a non-aggregate key.

findings.body:

`Or` explicitly handled a nil receiver by allocating a fresh status. `Combine` dereferences `st` unconditionally. Any caller that starts from `var status *charset.EscapeStatus`, as was valid with `Or`, will now panic at render time. There is no compile-time signal of this contract change; all three call sites in this diff (devtest, blame, view_file) depend on their accumulator being non-nil.

Suggestion: Add a doc comment stating the receiver must be non-nil, and ensure every accumulator is initialized as `&charset.EscapeStatus{}`. Alternatively, guard with `if other == nil { return }` and document the requirement for the receiver.

The declaration of `escapeStatus` is not in this diff, so this could not be verified. findings.title: In-place Combine depends on a non-nil pointer accumulator
findings.body:
The old code reassigned the result of `escapeStatus.Or(...)`, so it worked whatever the receiver's state, and `Or` could allocate or return a new value. The new `escapeStatus.Combine(...)` discards any return value and mutates the receiver in place. This is only correct under two conditions:
- `escapeStatus` must be initialized as a non-nil `*charset.EscapeStatus` before the loop.
- `Combine` must have a pointer receiver.

If `escapeStatus` is declared as a nil pointer, `Combine` will panic or silently do nothing. If `Combine` has a value receiver, the aggregation is lost. findings.title: Combine dereferences a nil receiver that Or used to tolerate
findings.body:
`Or` explicitly handled `status == nil` by allocating a fresh struct. findings.title: DefaultRetry budget is too short for quota contention
findings.body:
`retry.DefaultRetry` makes 5 attempts at about 10ms intervals with factor 1.0, roughly 50ms in total. The issue being worked around (kubernetes#67761) shows up when many objects in a namespace are created in parallel and all update the same ResourceQuota status. A ~50ms window with no exponential growth will often still exhaust under that load, so installs keep failing intermittently. They also now send 5x the PATCH traffic while doing so.

Suggestion: Use an exponential backoff, e.g. wait.Backoff{Steps: 5, Duration: 100 * time.Millisecond, Factor: 2.0, Jitter: 0.1}, or reuse retry.DefaultBackoff.

findings.title: hostWrapper hides optional host capability interfaces
findings.body:
`hostWrapper` embeds `component.Host`, so the only methods it promotes are those in the `component.Host` interface (`GetExtensions`). The concrete host passed in (`graph.Host` / the service host) also implements optional capability interfaces that extensions discover by type assertion, such as `hostcapabilities.ModuleInfo` (`GetModuleInfos`) and any other host capabilities.

Only `RegisterZPages` is re-exported. Every other assertion an extension makes on the host now fails. Extensions that rely on these capabilities (e.g. OpAMP or health/status extensions that read module info) stop working silently. This regresses every extension, not only those that report status.

Suggestion: Forward every capability interface the service host implements, e.g. `GetModuleInfos()` delegating via type assertion. Alternatively, give the graph host a per-component status-reporting view instead of hiding it behind a narrow wrapper. Add a test asserting that the wrapped host still satisfies the same capability interfaces as the original.

findings.title: Extensions can drive lifecycle states the service owns
findings.body:
`Report` forwards any event unfiltered to the FSM. If an extension reports `StatusOK`, `StatusStopping` or `StatusStopped` itself, it races with the service's own `ReportOKIfStarting` and Stopping/Stopped events. That race can produce invalid-transition errors or a misleading lifecycle state for the extension. Receivers and processors get the same treatment, so this may be acceptable. findings.title: Waiting for both directions can hang forever / leak goroutines
findings.body:
Previously, the first finished direction returned, and `defer srv.Close()` plus the caller's client close unblocked the other copy. Now handleTCP blocks until both copies finish, which breaks in two cases.

1. The wrappers report themselves as HalfClosers but fall back to a silent no-op when the inner conn cannot half-close (`connWithOneByte`, `sysConn`). In that case the peer never sees EOF and the other io.Copy blocks until the remote side chooses to close.
2. If one direction fails with a real error (e.g. the client resets), the other direction keeps waiting on a backend that may hold the connection open indefinitely.

Either way the handler, both goroutines and both sockets leak.

Suggestion: Fall back to a full close when either direction ends with a non-EOF error or when half-close is not actually supported. Alternatively, after the first result, apply a deadline or close the conns if the second direction does not finish.

Suggestion: Use an atomic.Bool for readClosed.

findings.title: Wrapper claims HalfCloser even when underlying conn can't half-close
findings.body:
`connWithOneByte` (and `sysConn` in tsdial) always satisfy `nettype.HalfCloser`, so `clientIsHalfCloser`/`srvIsHalfCloser` in socks5 is always true. findings.body: `handleTCP` used to return, and close both connections via the deferred `srv.Close()` and the caller, as soon as one direction finished. It now blocks until both directions finish, but a copy error does not close the other direction. If one `io.Copy` fails (for example a connection reset on the backend), the other goroutine can stay blocked in `Read` indefinitely, because the peer is never told to stop. The connection and goroutines then leak until the peer closes. The same happens when either side is not a `HalfCloser`: `CloseWrite` and `CloseRead` are no-ops, so EOF in one direction never propagates. `connWithOneByte` always satisfies the interface even when its inner `Conn` does not. Consider fully closing both connections when a copy returns a non-EOF error, or when half-close is unsupported.

findings.title: Default path ignores a reassigned or replaced process.env
findings.body:
The old code built the child's environment from `{ ...process.env }`, so whatever object `process.env` currently referenced was what the child inherited. `process.env` is a writable property, and test harnesses, dotenv-style loaders and sandboxes routinely assign a plain object or a Proxy to it. After such an assignment, the new fast path reads the real OS environment block via `getEnvPairs()`. Children then silently get the original environment instead of the one the program set up. This also defeats code that deliberately scrubs secrets by replacing `process.env`.

Suggestion: Only take the fast path when `process.env` is still the native env proxy. One way is to capture the original reference at module load (`const originalEnv = process.env`) and test `process.env === originalEnv`. Otherwise fall back to the copy-based path.
findings.label: defect:d1

findings.title: Default Pairs() can produce keys that differ from what Get() looked up
findings.body:
Keys are converted with `Utf8Value` and passed to `Get(const char*)`, which stops at the first NUL. For MapKVStore, which is used by workers with a custom `env`, a key containing an embedded NUL is looked up truncated. It may then resolve to a different variable's value, and the pair is emitted under the full key. The old JS path rejected such keys via `validateArgumentNullCheck`. This path skips that validation and passes NUL-containing strings to uv_spawn.

Suggestion: Skip, or reject, keys and values that contain '\0' in `KVStore::Pairs` so it matches the JS validation.
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Failure leaves undefined envPairs with no thrown exception guaranteed
findings.body:
If `Pairs()` returns an empty MaybeLocal, `getEnvPairs()` returns `undefined`. Nothing guarantees a pending exception, for example when the `Enumerate()` of a custom KVStore fails silently. The JS caller does not check the result. On Windows `dedupeWindowsEnvPairs(undefined)` then throws a confusing TypeError. On other platforms `undefined` envPairs reach `spawn` and may hit native CHECKs or spawn the child with an empty environment.

Suggestion: In JS, verify `envPairs` is an array and fall back to the copy path if it is not. Alternatively, in C++, throw an explicit error when `Pairs()` fails without a pending exception.
findings.label: invalid

findings.title: Fast path skips null-byte validation for non-real env stores
findings.body:
The fast path assumes entries cannot contain NUL bytes because they come from the real environment block. That is not true in Worker threads without `SHARE_ENV`: `env_vars()` is a `MapKVStore`, and a value like `process.env.X = 'a\0b'` is stored verbatim. The old path rejected it with `ERR_INVALID_ARG_VALUE` via `validateArgumentNullCheck`. The new path silently passes a string with an embedded NUL to `uv_spawn`, which truncates it at the C level.

Suggestion: Limit the fast path to the main-thread real env store, or validate the returned pairs for '\0' (cheap with StringPrototypeIncludes) and throw the same error as before.

findings.title: Default env no longer includes enumerable prototype properties
findings.body:
Previously `{ ...process.env }` was iterated with `for...in`, which the code comments say intentionally includes enumerable `Object.prototype` properties. Those were passed to the child even with no `options.env`. The fast path drops them, so the default env and an explicit `{ ...process.env }` now behave differently. This is an undocumented semantic change that the new test does not cover.

Suggestion: Either note it as an intentional behavior change (with a test) or append enumerable inherited keys in the fast path to keep parity.

findings.title: Windows dedupe can pick a different value than the old path
findings.body:
The old code deduplicated key names, then read `env[key]` through the case-insensitive Windows `process.env` getter. For case-variant duplicates such as `Path`/`PATH`, the value therefore came from `GetEnvironmentVariableW`'s first match. The new code keeps the raw value attached to the lexicographically-first name. When the duplicates hold different values, the child can now inherit a different value than before.

Suggestion: For keys that collide case-insensitively, resolve the value the same way the old path did (via the store's Get), or document and test the new semantics explicitly.

findings.title: RealEnvStore::Pairs lacks its own EscapableHandleScope
findings.body:
The base `KVStore::Pairs` opens an `EscapableHandleScope`, but the override creates one handle per env var in the caller's scope. That works when the caller is a FunctionCallback. It is inconsistent with the base implementation and leaks handles into whatever scope a future caller uses.

Suggestion: Add `EscapableHandleScope scope(isolate);` and `return scope.Escape(Array::New(...));`.
findings.label: nit

findings.title: Default env no longer de-duplicates repeated variable names on POSIX
findings.body:
The old path built `{ ...process.env }`, which collapses repeated names to a single key. The value was whatever `getenv()` returns, which is the first occurrence. `RealEnvStore::Pairs` copies every `uv_os_environ()` entry verbatim instead. If the parent was exec'd with duplicate entries (e.g. `A=1` and `A=2` passed through `execve`), the child now receives both, but `process.env.A` in the parent shows only `1`. Programs resolve duplicates differently: some take the first entry, some the last. So what the parent sees and what the child uses can now diverge, which is a classic environment-confusion hazard. The new code comment claims this path matches copying `process.env`, but it does not.

Suggestion: Skip names already emitted, e.g. keep a `std::unordered_set<std::string>` of names and `continue` on repeats. That keeps the first occurrence, matching `getenv()` and the previous object-copy semantics.

findings.title: Hoist GetCurrentContext out of the loop

`isolate->GetCurrentContext()` runs once per variable while the global env mutex is held. The context does not change during the loop, so this is avoidable work inside the critical section.

Suggestion: Local<Context> context = isolate->GetCurrentContext(); // before the loop, then use `context` in ToV8Value

findings.title: Fast path ignores a reassigned or wrapped process.env
findings.body:
`process.env` is a writable property. Code and tools routinely do `process.env = { ...custom }`, or replace it with a Proxy or a getter-based object (dotenv-style loaders, test harnesses).

The old default built the child env from whatever `process.env` currently referenced. The new path calls `getEnvPairs()`, which reads `env->env_vars()` natively. A child spawned without `options.env` now silently gets the original OS environment instead of the user's replacement. That is a behavior regression, and it can leak variables the user intended to strip, such as secrets.

Suggestion: Take the fast path only when `process.env` is still the original env proxy. For example, capture the original object at bootstrap and check `process.env === originalProcessEnv`; otherwise fall back to the JS copy.

findings.title: Generic Pairs() skips the null-byte validation the JS path performed
findings.body:
For workers, `env_vars()` is a MapKVStore whose `std::string` values can contain embedded NULs (e.g. `process.env.X = 'a\0b=c'`). The old path rejected these with `validateArgumentNullCheck` (ERR_INVALID_ARG_VALUE).

The new default path forwards such pairs straight to uv_spawn, which treats them as C strings. The variable is silently truncated instead of raising an error.

Separately, `Get(*key_utf8)` looks the key up as a C string while `pair.assign(*key_utf8, length)` uses the full length. A key with an embedded NUL therefore pairs the name with the wrong value.

Suggestion: In `KVStore::Pairs`, skip or reject entries whose key or value contains '\0'. Alternatively, restrict the JS fast path to the main thread with the real env store, and keep the validated JS path for workers.

- Before this PR, it threw `ERR_INVALID_ARG_VALUE`.
- Now the value is passed through and silently truncated at the NUL when converted to a C string for `uv_spawn`.

findings.title: Null-byte check dropped
findings.body: The comment says entries cannot contain null bytes, but that holds only for the real OS environment. In a Worker without `SHARE_ENV`, `process.env` is backed by a `MapKVStore`, and the default `KVStore::Pairs()` builds pairs from those strings. Keys and values are stored with their full length, so a null byte can be present. Previously `validateArgumentNullCheck` threw `ERR_INVALID_ARG_VALUE`. Now the pair reaches `uv_spawn()` and is silently truncated at the null byte. Whether a worker can actually store such a value depends on `MapKVStore::Set`, which I did not see in this diff.

findings.title: Behavior Change
findings.body: The default-env path now reads the native env store through `getEnvPairs()` and no longer reads the JS-visible `process.env`. The old code copied `{ ...process.env }`, so it also honored a replaced `process.env` object (e.g. `process.env = { FOO: 'bar' }`). Under the new code a child spawned without `options.env` inherits the real environment block instead of that object. The same applies to any other property or getter-based override of `process.env`. I am not certain this pattern is supported or tested in the repo, so verify it. If it is supported, either keep the old path when `process.env` is not the native env proxy, or document the change.
findings.label: defect:d1

findings.title: Synchronous throws in pump() leave the request pending and inFlight stuck
findings.body:
`pump` calls `stream.read()`, reads `chunk.then` and calls `then` with no try/catch. When `pump` runs from the `PromisePrototypeThen(new Promise(wakeup), ...)` continuation, any throw only rejects that internal promise. The result is an unhandled rejection; the caller's `resolve`/`reject` are never invoked and `inFlight` remains `true`, so the iterator hangs. When `pump` runs via `drain()`, the throw propagates synchronously into whatever triggered the drain. The thenable multiple-callback problem also applies here: each callback sets `inFlight = false` and drains. Previously such errors were caught by the generator's catch block, aggregated into `error`, and the stream was destroyed.

Suggestion: Wrap the body of `pump` in try/catch, set `inFlight = false` on throw, call `settleError(err, reject)` and then drain. Guard the `then` callbacks with a once-flag, or assimilate via `PromiseResolve(chunk)`.
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Fast path returns the raw result of a user `then` instead of a promise
findings.body:
For a thenable chunk, `next()` returns whatever the chunk's own `then` returns. Several failures follow from this:
- A non-native thenable can return `undefined` or a non-promise. `for await` then gets a non-object iterator result and throws a TypeError.
- If `then` throws synchronously, `next()` throws instead of rejecting. `inFlight` stays `true` forever, so every later `next()`/`return()`/`throw()` is queued and never served. The stream is also never finalized.
- A thenable that invokes its callbacks more than once, or both of them, re-runs `onChunkFulfilled`/`onChunkRejected`. That clears `inFlight` while another request may be in flight, and calls `finalize()` again.

The old `yield chunk` went through spec `PromiseResolve`/Await, which assimilates thenables safely and routes all of these cases into the try/catch/finally.

Suggestion: Assimilate through a native promise instead of calling `then` directly, so throws, multiple calls and odd return values are handled by the engine. For example:

`inFlight = true; return PromisePrototypeThen(PromiseResolve(chunk), onChunkFulfilled, onChunkRejected);`

Also wrap the `chunk.then` access in try/catch.
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Fast-path read()/then getter exceptions bypass teardown
findings.body:
In `next()`, a throw from `stream.read()` (for example from a decoder) or from a throwing `then` getter escapes as a synchronous exception rather than a rejected promise. The iterator is not completed and the stream is neither destroyed nor detached from (the `readable`/eos listeners stay attached). The old generator turned these into a rejection and ran the `finally` cleanup.

Suggestion: Wrap the fast path in try/catch. On error, aggregate it into `error`, call `finalize()` and return `PromiseReject(error)`.
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Exceptions inside pump() become unhandled rejections and hang the request
findings.body:
`pump` runs from `PromisePrototypeThen(new Promise(wakeup), () => pump(resolve, reject))` (lines 1534 and 1598). If `stream.read()`, the `then` getter, or the `then` call throws, the derived promise rejects and nothing handles it. That can crash the process under the default unhandled-rejection mode. The original `resolve`/`reject` are never called and `inFlight` stays true, so the consumer hangs and all queued requests are stranded.

Suggestion: Guard pump's body with try/catch: `catch (err) { inFlight = false; settleError(err, reject); if (queue !== null) drain(); }`.
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Synchronous exceptions escape next() and bypass finalize()
findings.body:
Several calls in the fast path can throw synchronously: `start()` (`eos`), `stream.read()` (which can throw from `_read`), the `chunk.then` getter, and the `then` call. Previously the generator's try/catch turned these into a rejected promise, recorded the error and ran `finally` to destroy or detach. Now `next()` throws synchronously and the stream is never cleaned up. If `then` throws after `inFlight = true`, the iterator is stuck: every later request is queued forever.

Suggestion: Wrap the body of next() in try/catch. On error, reset `inFlight`, call `settleError` (aggregate the error, finalize), and return a rejected promise.
findings.label: valid

findings.title: next() returns the thenable's return value instead of a promise
findings.body:
The fast path returns `FunctionPrototypeCall(then, chunk, onChunkFulfilled, onChunkRejected)`. That only works when `chunk.then` behaves like a native Promise and returns a derived promise. A custom thenable (e.g. `{ then(cb) { cb(1); } }`) returns `undefined`, so `next()` returns `undefined`. `for await` then fails with a TypeError and `await it.next()` gives the wrong result. The old `yield` awaited the value with full Promise Resolution semantics.

Suggestion: Wrap the delivery in a real promise, e.g. `return new Promise((resolve, reject) => FunctionPrototypeCall(then, chunk, (v) => { ...; resolve({ done: false, value: v }); }, (e) => { ...; settleError(e, reject); }));`, or use `PromisePrototypeThen(PromiseResolve(chunk), onChunkFulfilled, onChunkRejected)`.
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Misbehaving thenables can settle twice and corrupt inFlight state
findings.body:
Nothing guards against a thenable calling its fulfill or reject callback more than once, or calling both. A second call sets `inFlight = false` and re-enters `drain()` while a later request may already be in flight. That breaks the one-request-at-a-time invariant and can interleave `stream.read()` calls or finalize twice. Native promise resolution guarantees at-most-once; the hand-rolled path does not. The same applies to `onChunkFulfilled`/`onChunkRejected`.

Suggestion: Use a local `let called = false` guard in the callbacks, or route through `PromiseResolve(chunk)`.
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Fast path duplicates pump() logic
findings.body:
The fast path in `next()` re-implements the read / thenable / error / end branching from `pump()` with different inFlight bookkeeping and different thenable handling (it returns `then()`'s result instead of resolving). The two copies have already diverged, and fixes must be applied twice.

Suggestion: Have next() create the promise once and call `processNext(resolve, reject)` when not inFlight, so there is a single code path.

findings.title: Queued requests can settle before the request ahead of them
findings.body:
`onChunkFulfilled` and `onChunkRejected` call `drain()` synchronously before returning or throwing. Queued requests can therefore be resolved, or the iterator finalized, before the promise returned by `then()` for the earlier request settles. Observers using `Promise.race`, or `.then` handlers registered in request order, see results out of order. This contradicts the comment that queued requests are "processed in order". The `pump()` path calls `resolve` before `drain()`, so the two paths also behave inconsistently.

Suggestion: Use the same explicit `new Promise` / `resolve`-then-`drain` structure as `pump()` for the fast-path thenable case, so the earlier request is always settled first.

findings.title: Fast path duplicates pump() logic
findings.body:
The `next()` fast path re-implements the read, thenable, error, and end branches of `pump()` with slightly different state handling (`inFlight` timing, settle order). The two copies have already diverged, and fixes to one (such as the throw-safety issues above) must be mirrored in the other. This is a likely source of future subtle bugs in a hot, correctness-critical path.

Suggestion: Have the fast path call a shared helper that, given `(resolve, reject)`, performs one read attempt. The fast path then only avoids allocating the waiting promise, while all settlement logic lives in one place.

findings.title: Synchronous throws in pump()/read() leave requests unsettled
findings.body:
The old generator wrapped `stream.read()` and `yield` in try/catch/finally. Any throw was aggregated into `error`, rejected the `next()` promise and destroyed or detached the stream. The new code has no equivalent.

In `pump()`, if `stream.read()` throws (for example a user `_read` or a `then` call throwing synchronously), the throw happens inside `PromisePrototypeThen(new Promise(wakeup), () => pump(...))`. That produces an unhandled rejection. `resolve`/`reject` are never called and `inFlight` stays true, so the consumer hangs and the stream is never finalized.

The same throw in the fast path (`stream.read()` at line 1575) escapes `next()` synchronously, skips `finalize()`, and leaves the 'readable' and eos listeners attached. When it happens inside `drain()`, it aborts the drain loop and strands the remaining queued requests.

Suggestion: Wrap the body of `pump()` (and the fast-path read) in try/catch. On a throw, set `inFlight = false`, call `settleError(err, reject)` (or return `PromiseReject` after `finalize()` in the fast path), and then call `drain()`.

findings.title: Fast path returns the user `then` result instead of a promise
findings.body:
For a thenable chunk, `next()` returns `FunctionPrototypeCall(then, chunk, onChunkFulfilled, onChunkRejected)` directly. This is only correct for native promises. A custom thenable (any object with a `then` method, common in objectMode) can return `undefined`, a non-promise or another thenable. `for await` then fails with "Iterator result undefined is not an object", or it receives a value that never settles in the iterator's own terms.

If `then` throws synchronously (a throwing getter is guarded, but the call itself is not), the exception escapes `next()` synchronously instead of becoming a rejected promise. Because `inFlight` was set to true just before the call, every later `next()`, `return()` and `throw()` is queued forever, so the iterator deadlocks and the stream is never finalized.

Suggestion: Always wrap the result in a fresh promise and route both settlement and synchronous throws through it:
```js
inFlight = true;
return new Promise((resolve, reject) => pump(resolve, reject));
```
or wrap the call in `new Promise((res, rej) => { try { FunctionPrototypeCall(then, chunk, v => res(onChunkFulfilled(v)), e => { try { onChunkRejected(e); } catch (x) { rej(x); } }); } catch (e) { inFlight = false; settleError(e, rej); } })`.
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Misbehaving thenables can corrupt the inFlight state
findings.body:
The fulfillment/rejection handlers passed to a user `then` unconditionally set `inFlight = false` and call `drain()`. A non-conforming thenable that invokes its callbacks more than once, or invokes both, will reset `inFlight` while a later request is already in flight. That starts a second concurrent `pump()`. The two pumps then share the single `callback` slot used by `wakeup`, so one waiter overwrites the other and one request never settles. Native `await`/`yield` protected against this by adopting the thenable through a one-shot promise capability.

Suggestion: Adopt the thenable through a real promise (e.g. `PromisePrototypeThen(new Promise((res, rej) => FunctionPrototypeCall(then, chunk, res, rej)), onFulfilled, onRejected)`) so the callbacks fire at most once.
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Test rewritten to accommodate changed scheduling
findings.body:
The old test asserted that aborting in a microtask happens before any mapper is invoked (`mustNotCall`). The rewrite now expects two mappers to run. The new iterator's synchronous fast path delivers chunks earlier than the async generator did, so this test was adjusted to fit that observable timing change rather than confirming the old behaviour still holds. This hides a user-visible change in microtask ordering for stream operators, and it should be called out (e.g. semver-major review or a doc note) rather than silently absorbed.

Suggestion: Keep a variant of the original assertion, or document the timing change in the PR and changelog, so the behaviour difference is reviewed explicitly.

findings.title: Non-promise thenables
findings.body:
On the fast path for a thenable chunk, `next()` returns whatever `chunk.then(...)` returns. Native promises return a promise, so they work. A spec-compliant custom thenable such as `{ then(res) { res(1) } }` returns `undefined` (or any non-promise value), so `next()` stops returning a promise. `for await` then fails with "Iterator result undefined is not an object".

The old async generator awaited any thenable correctly. A fix is to wrap the call, for example `new Promise((res, rej) => then.call(chunk, res, rej))`, or to resolve the value through a native promise before chaining.

findings.title: Sync throw/hang
findings.body:
This affects both the `chunk.then` getter and the `then` call itself.

- **Fast path:** if either throws, `next()` throws synchronously instead of returning a rejected promise. `inFlight` has already been set to `true`, so every later `next()`/`return()`/`throw()` is queued forever and the stream is never finalized or destroyed.
- **Waiting path (`pump()`):** the same throw happens inside a `.then` callback. It becomes an unhandled rejection, and the caller's `next()` promise never settles.

The old generator caught this in its `try` block, which set the error and destroyed the stream. The throw should be caught and routed through `settleError`/`onChunkRejected`.

findings.title: Multi-settling thenable
findings.body:
In `pump()`, the callbacks passed to a custom thenable are not guarded against being called more than once, or calling both fulfil and reject. A misbehaving thenable could do either.

- Each call resets `inFlight = false` and calls `drain()`. If this happens while a later request is already in flight, the serialization invariant breaks: two pumps may run at once and overwrite the shared `callback`.
- A rejection may also `finalize()` the stream after a value was already delivered.

Native promises are unaffected. Guard the callbacks with a `settled` flag.

findings.title: Thenable contract broken
findings.body:
For a buffered thenable chunk, `next()` returns the raw result of the chunk's `then` call instead of a promise it controls. The previous async generator awaited the chunk, which tolerated all of the cases below. With a non-native thenable in an objectMode stream, each case breaks:
- If `then` returns `undefined` or a non-promise, `next()` breaks the async iterator protocol and `for await` throws a TypeError.
- If `then` throws synchronously, or a getter on `then` throws, `next()` throws instead of rejecting.
- In either case `inFlight` stays `true` forever, so every later `next()`, `return()` or `throw()` is queued and never settles.
Wrap the call so the result is always a fresh promise, for example by resolving inside `new Promise` with a `try`/`catch` that resets `inFlight` and calls `settleError`.

findings.title: Hang on throwing then
findings.body:
In `pump()`, the chunk's `then` is read and called with no `try`/`catch`. The same applies to the `chunk.then` getter.
- When `pump()` runs from the `() => pump(resolve, reject)` reaction after waiting for `'readable'`, a synchronous throw only rejects the discarded derived promise. That causes an unhandled rejection, and the request's `resolve`/`reject` are never called.
- When `pump()` runs from `drain()`, the throw propagates out of the caller.
In both paths `inFlight` stays `true`, so the iterator hangs and the stream is never finalized. A thenable that never calls its callbacks also hangs, but a synchronous throw should at least reject via `settleError`.
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Out-of-order settlement
findings.body:
In the fast-path thenable case, `onChunkFulfilled` calls `drain()` before returning the value. Queued requests are therefore resolved before the promise returned by the first `next()` settles.
This only matters when `next()` is called concurrently without awaiting, for example with `Promise.race` or reactions attached to both promises. The second request's reactions can then run before the first's. This contradicts the in-order guarantee described in the comment.
The `pump()` path avoids this by calling `resolve` before `drain()`. Consider making the fast path resolve the first request before draining as well.

findings.title: Same `chunk.then` crash on `undefined` chunks in pump()
findings.body:
When data arrives after waiting, `pump` reads `chunk.then` without a null/undefined guard. An `undefined` objectMode chunk throws inside the `.then` callback of `PromisePrototypeThen(new Promise(wakeup), ...)`. The `next()` promise never settles, `inFlight` stays true, and the queued requests never drain. The error surfaces only as an unhandled rejection.

findings.title: Chunk of `undefined` crashes the iterator on `chunk.then`
findings.body:
In objectMode, `push(undefined)` is accepted and `read()` returns `undefined`, which passes the `chunk !== null` check. The new code then reads `chunk.then`, which throws a TypeError. The old generator simply yielded `undefined`. In the fast path `next()` throws synchronously instead of returning a rejected promise, and the iterator is left started but unfinalized. The same access in `pump` (line 1506) throws inside a promise callback instead, which hangs the request (see the separate finding on the unhandled `.then` chain).

Suggestion: Guard the access: `const then = chunk != null ? chunk.then : undefined;` in both `next()` and `pump()`.

findings.title: Exceptions in pump() after wakeup are swallowed and leave the request hanging
findings.body:
`pump` is invoked from `PromisePrototypeThen(new Promise(wakeup), () => pump(...))` with no rejection handler. If `stream.read()` or the thenable handling throws, the derived promise rejects unhandled. The outer `next()` promise never settles and `inFlight` stays true, so all queued requests hang. The same pattern is at line 1598. The old async generator propagated such errors to the consumer.

Suggestion: Wrap the body in try/catch and route the error through `inFlight = false; settleError(err, reject); drain()`, or pass a rejection handler to `PromisePrototypeThen`.

findings.title: next() returns the raw result of a foreign thenable's then()
findings.body:
The fast path returns whatever `then.call(chunk, onFulfilled, onRejected)` yields. For a native promise that is a promise of the iterator result. For a custom thenable, `then` may return `undefined` or something else. `next()` would then return a non-promise, which breaks the async iterator contract, and the `{done:false,value}` result would be lost. A thenable that throws synchronously also makes `next()` throw instead of reject, with `inFlight` stuck at true. Non-native thenables should be wrapped so that `next()` always returns a promise that settles from the callbacks.

Suggestion: Wrap it: `return new Promise((resolve, reject) => { inFlight = true; FunctionPrototypeCall(then, chunk, (v) => { onChunkFulfilled(v); resolve({done:false,value:v}); }, (e) => { try { onChunkRejected(e); } catch (x) { reject(x); } }); });`

findings.title: next() returns the thenable's raw `then()` result instead of a Promise
findings.body:
For a thenable chunk, `next()` returns whatever `then.call(chunk, onChunkFulfilled, onChunkRejected)` returns. Native promises return a derived promise, but a custom thenable (`{ then(res) { res(1) } }`) usually returns `undefined`. `next()` then returns `undefined` and the `{done:false,value}` produced by `onChunkFulfilled` is discarded. Consumers calling `.then` on the result or using `for await` would break. The old async generator awaited yielded values through the spec's promise-resolve machinery, so this is a regression. Thenables that call the callbacks more than once or after settling are also not guarded.

Suggestion: Normalize through a real promise: `return new Promise((resolve, reject) => { inFlight = true; then.call(chunk, (v) => { inFlight = false; resolve({ done: false, value: v }); if (queue !== null) drain(); }, (e) => { inFlight = false; settleError(e, reject); if (queue !== null) drain(); }); });`. This is the same shape `pump` already uses. Alternatively use `PromiseResolve(chunk)` first.

findings.title: Queued requests settle before the request that was ahead of them
findings.body:
`onChunkFulfilled` and `onChunkRejected` call `drain()` before returning or throwing. Queued requests are resolved synchronously inside `drain()`, while the promise for the current request is only settled after the callback returns, via promise-chain resolution. Requests behind it can therefore be settled first, and their reactions run before the current request's reactions. On the rejection path, a queued `next()` can resolve `{done:true}` before the preceding `next()` rejects with the error. This breaks the in-order guarantee the iterator advertises, and it differs from `pump`'s thenable path, which resolves first and drains afterwards.

Suggestion: Settle the current request first, then drain. Use the explicit resolve/reject pattern from `pump` for the fast path as well.

findings.title: Synchronous throws leave the iterator stuck in-flight or throw from next()
findings.body:
`stream.read()` (which can throw, for example from a custom `_read`/transform path) and `chunk.then` (a throwing getter, or `undefined` as a chunk in object mode, which gives a TypeError) are evaluated directly in `next()`. A throw there makes `next()` throw synchronously instead of returning a rejected promise. If `inFlight = true` was already set (line 1581 and the `then` call), it is never reset. In `pump`, called from the `.then(() => pump(...))` wakeup callback, a throw becomes an unhandled rejection. The outer request promise never settles and `inFlight` stays true, so every later request queues forever. The async generator turned all of these into a rejection plus cleanup.

Suggestion: Wrap the read/then access in try/catch and route failures through `settleError`. Guard `chunk.then` for null/undefined chunks (`chunk != null && typeof chunk.then === 'function'`). Wrap `pump` calls from the wakeup callback so errors reject the request and reset `inFlight`.

findings.title: Duplicated read/settle logic between next() fast path and pump()
findings.body:
The read, thenable detection, error/end handling and wait logic are implemented twice (in `next()` and `pump()`) with subtly different settle ordering and error handling. The thenable bugs above exist only in the `next()` copy. Keeping two copies of this state machine invites further divergence.

Suggestion: Make `next()` allocate the promise and call `processNext` directly, or share one helper that takes `resolve`/`reject` and keeps the sync fast path only for the already-resolved result.

findings.title: Queued requests are settled before the request that was in flight
findings.body:
`onChunkFulfilled` calls `drain()` before returning `{ done: false, value }`. `drain()` can synchronously resolve queued requests, so the promise for a later `next()` becomes fulfilled before the promise for the earlier request. The earlier promise is only resolved after this callback returns. Consumers that observe resolution order, for example with `Promise.race` or reactions attached directly to the promises, see out-of-order settlement. The slow path in `pump()` resolves first and then drains, so the two paths are inconsistent.

Suggestion: Defer the drain until after the current promise has been resolved. For example, return a value from the callback and call `drain()` in a following microtask, or use the `pump()`-style structure that resolves explicitly and then drains.

findings.title: Exceptions in the wake-up retry are unhandled and leave the iterator stuck

`pump` is re-run from a `.then()` callback whose resulting promise nobody handles. If `pump` throws (for example `stream.read()` throwing, or the `chunk.then` access), the outer promise returned to the caller is never resolved or rejected. `inFlight` stays true, so every later `next()` is queued forever, and an unhandled rejection is raised. The async generator surfaced these errors through the iteration. The same pattern appears at line 1598.

Suggestion: Catch errors in the retry, for example `PromisePrototypeThen(new Promise(wakeup), () => pump(resolve, reject)).catch(...)`, or wrap the body of `pump` in try/catch that sets `inFlight = false`, calls `settleError(err, reject)` and then drains the queue.

findings.title: Fast-path thenable handling returns whatever `then()` returns and is not idempotent
findings.body:
`next()` returns the result of calling a user-supplied `then` directly. Only native promises return a promise from `then`. A non-native thenable can return `undefined`, so `next()` would not return a promise, which breaks the async iterator contract. A misbehaving thenable can also call `onChunkFulfilled` or `onChunkRejected` more than once, or both. Each call re-runs `inFlight = false` and `drain()`, and the rejected callback also re-runs `finalize()`. The slow path in `pump()` has the same lack of a once-only guard.

Suggestion: Wrap the thenable in a real promise: `return new Promise((res, rej) => FunctionPrototypeCall(then, chunk, res, rej)).then(onChunkFulfilled, onChunkRejected);` or use `PromiseResolve(chunk)` once the `then` check has passed. The wrapper settles only once.

findings.title: ESLint `no-require-imports` fires on the new `require('internal/fixed_queue')`
findings.body:
The linter forbids `require()` imports. This file is a CommonJS internal module and uses `require` for every other dependency, such as `string_decoder` and `internal/streams/from` on the adjacent lines. The warning is therefore a rule/config mismatch, not a real defect in this change. Leaving it unaddressed adds lint noise or breaks a lint gate that applies the TypeScript rule set to this file.

Suggestion: Keep `require` for consistency with the file and exclude `lib/internal/**` from `@typescript-eslint/no-require-imports` in the lint config. Alternatively add `// eslint-disable-next-line @typescript-eslint/no-require-imports` above the line. Do not mix in ESM `import`.

findings.title: Queued requests are drained before the current request's promise is settled
findings.body:
`onChunkFulfilled` and `onChunkRejected` call `drain()` before returning or throwing. `drain()` synchronously resolves later queued `next()` promises, and only after that does the current request's promise settle from the handler's return value. A later request can therefore settle before an earlier one. A consumer doing `p1.then(a); p2.then(b)` can observe `b` before `a`. For `onChunkRejected`, a queued `next()` can resolve `{done: true}` before the rejection that caused it is delivered. The `pump()` thenable path avoids this by calling `resolve` first and then `drain()`.

Suggestion: Make the fast thenable path settle through explicit resolve/reject callbacks, as `pump()` does. For example, wrap it in `new Promise((resolve, reject) => FunctionPrototypeCall(then, chunk, v => { inFlight = false; resolve({done:false, value:v}); drain(); }, e => { inFlight = false; settleError(e, reject); drain(); }))`. Alternatively, defer `drain()` to a microtask that runs after the settle.
