findings.title: Set content length on retried uploads
findings.body:
`s.f.srv.Call` returns a non-error response for HTTP 4xx/5xx statuses only if the rest client treats them as errors. If `opts.ContentLength` is not set, a fresh `bytes.NewReader` body may be sent chunked, which breaks presigned S3 PUT uploads. Set `ContentLength` explicitly for each attempt so retries send a correct length.

Improved code:
body := chunk.Bytes()
opts.Body = bytes.NewReader(body)
contentLength := int64(len(body))
opts.ContentLength = &contentLength
uploadRes, err = s.f.srv.Call(ctx, &opts)
return shouldRetry(ctx, uploadRes, err)

findings.title: Possible Hang
findings.body:
`handleTCP` now waits for both copy goroutines before returning, so the deferred `srv.Close()` runs only after both finish. When one direction ends, only a half-close is propagated. The other `io.Copy` stays blocked until that peer closes its side.

If either conn is not a `nettype.HalfCloser`, nothing unblocks the second copy. This happens with a custom `Server.Dialer` returning a non-TCP conn, or with `connWithOneByte` wrapping a non-TCP conn, where the methods are silent no-ops. Previously the first finishing direction tore down both sides. Now the goroutines and connections can leak indefinitely, for example after a backend reset or full close while the client keeps its socket open.

Fall back to fully closing both conns when half-close is unsupported, or after an error in either direction.

`handleTCP` used to return after the first direction finished, and `defer srv.Close()` then tore everything down. It now waits for both copies, which can hang in two cases:

findings.title: Idle becomes force-close
findings.body:
On native servers with `forceCloseConnections: 'idle'`, the new condition skips the first branch because `options.serverFactory` is not set. Execution then falls through to `else if (serverHasCloseAllConnections && forceCloseConnections)`. Since `'idle'` is a truthy string, `instance.server.closeAllConnections()` now runs.

As a result, the `'idle'` mode, whose purpose is to close only idle keep-alive sockets, now aborts in-flight requests on every default Fastify server during `close()`. The fix should keep `'idle'` out of the force-close branch, for example by nesting the `serverFactory` check inside the `'idle'` branch or by making the else-if check `forceCloseConnections === true`.

findings.title: Null-byte check skipped
findings.body:
The fast path skips `validateArgumentNullCheck` because the real environment block cannot contain null bytes. `getEnvPairs()` uses the per-`Environment` store, though, and inside a Worker that is a `MapKVStore` (unless `SHARE_ENV` is used).

`MapKVStore::Set` keeps embedded NULs. So in a worker, `process.env.FOO = 'a\0b'` followed by `spawn(cmd)` now behaves differently:
- Before this PR, it threw `ERR_INVALID_ARG_VALUE`.
- Now the value is passed through and silently truncated at the NUL when converted to a C string for `uv_spawn`.

A key containing a NUL is also silently dropped, because `Get(*key_utf8)` looks it up with a truncated `const char*`. The fix is to keep the null check for non-real stores, or to validate in `KVStore::Pairs`.
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Truncated key lookup
findings.body:
The default `KVStore::Pairs` looks up each key with `Get(*key_utf8)`, which takes a `const char*`. Any key with an embedded NUL (possible in `MapKVStore`) is therefore looked up under a truncated name. The result is either that the key is skipped, or that the value of a different key (the prefix) is emitted under the full key name.

Using the `Local<String>` `Get` overload, or a length-aware lookup, would avoid this mismatch.

findings.title: Behavior Change
findings.body:
The default (no `options.env`) path no longer includes inherited enumerable properties. The old code iterated the `{ ...process.env }` copy with `for...in`, and the comment says "Prototype values are intentionally included". That loop also picked up enumerable properties added to `Object.prototype`, and those values reached the child's environment. `getEnvPairs()` returns only the real environment block, so these properties are now silently dropped.

Not inheriting prototype pollution is arguably the better behavior. Still, the default spawn environment is observably different, and the PR describes the change as a pure optimization. It should be called out explicitly, possibly labeled, and covered by a test such as `Object.prototype.X = 'y'` followed by `spawnSync()` with no `env`, so the new semantics are deliberate rather than accidental.

findings.title: Duplicate Entries
findings.body:
On POSIX, `RealEnvStore::Pairs()` forwards every `uv_os_environ()` entry as-is. A process can be started with duplicate names in its environment block (e.g. via `execve` with `FOO=a` and `FOO=b`). The old path collapsed these into one key through the object spread, using the value `getenv()` returns. The new path passes both entries to the child, which can then resolve `FOO` differently than the parent's `process.env.FOO`.

This is narrow, but it is a difference from the PR's claim that the result matches a copy of `process.env`. Windows is not affected because `dedupeWindowsEnvPairs()` filters duplicates there.

findings.title: Non-promise thenables
findings.body:
On the fast path for a thenable chunk, `next()` returns whatever `chunk.then(...)` returns. Native promises return a promise, so they work. A spec-compliant custom thenable such as `{ then(res) { res(1) } }` returns `undefined` (or any non-promise value), so `next()` stops returning a promise. `for await` then fails with "Iterator result undefined is not an object".

The old async generator awaited any thenable correctly. A fix is to wrap the call, for example `new Promise((res, rej) => then.call(chunk, res, rej))`, or to resolve the value through a native promise before chaining.
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Sync throw/hang
findings.body:
This affects both the `chunk.then` getter and the `then` call itself.

- **Fast path:** if either throws, `next()` throws synchronously instead of returning a rejected promise. `inFlight` has already been set to `true`, so every later `next()`/`return()`/`throw()` is queued forever and the stream is never finalized or destroyed.
- **Waiting path (`pump()`):** the same throw happens inside a `.then` callback. It becomes an unhandled rejection, and the caller's `next()` promise never settles.

The old generator caught this in its `try` block, which set the error and destroyed the stream. The throw should be caught and routed through `settleError`/`onChunkRejected`.
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Multi-settling thenable
findings.body:
In `pump()`, the callbacks passed to a custom thenable are not guarded against being called more than once, or calling both fulfil and reject. A misbehaving thenable could do either.

- Each call resets `inFlight = false` and calls `drain()`. If this happens while a later request is already in flight, the serialization invariant breaks: two pumps may run at once and overwrite the shared `callback`.
- A rejection may also `finalize()` the stream after a value was already delivered.

Native promises are unaffected. Guard the callbacks with a `settled` flag.

findings.title: Thenable contract broken
findings.body:
For a buffered thenable chunk, `next()` returns the raw result of the chunk's `then` call instead of a promise it controls. The previous async generator awaited the chunk, which tolerated all of the cases below. With a non-native thenable in an objectMode stream, each case breaks:
- If `then` returns `undefined` or a non-promise, `next()` breaks the async iterator protocol and `for await` throws a TypeError.
- If `then` throws synchronously, or a getter on `then` throws, `next()` throws instead of rejecting.
- In either case `inFlight` stays `true` forever, so every later `next()`, `return()` or `throw()` is queued and never settles.
Wrap the call so the result is always a fresh promise, for example by resolving inside `new Promise` with a `try`/`catch` that resets `inFlight` and calls `settleError`.
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Hang on throwing then
findings.body:
In `pump()`, the chunk's `then` is read and called with no `try`/`catch`. The same applies to the `chunk.then` getter.
- When `pump()` runs from the `() => pump(resolve, reject)` reaction after waiting for `'readable'`, a synchronous throw only rejects the discarded derived promise. That causes an unhandled rejection, and the request's `resolve`/`reject` are never called.
- When `pump()` runs from `drain()`, the throw propagates out of the caller.
In both paths `inFlight` stays `true`, so the iterator hangs and the stream is never finalized. A thenable that never calls its callbacks also hangs, but a synchronous throw should at least reject via `settleError`.
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Out-of-order settlement
findings.body:
In the fast-path thenable case, `onChunkFulfilled` calls `drain()` before returning the value. Queued requests are therefore resolved before the promise returned by the first `next()` settles.
This only matters when `next()` is called concurrently without awaiting, for example with `Promise.race` or reactions attached to both promises. The second request's reactions can then run before the first's. This contradicts the in-order guarantee described in the comment.
The `pump()` path avoids this by calling `resolve` before `drain()`. Consider making the fast path resolve the first request before draining as well.

findings.body: On the fast path, `next()` returns whatever `then.call(chunk, onChunkFulfilled, onChunkRejected)` returns. That is only a promise when the chunk is a native promise. A custom thenable (`{ then(res) { res(1) } }`) usually returns `undefined`, so `next()` returns a non-promise. `await it.next()` then yields `undefined`, and destructuring `{ value, done }` throws, or the result is otherwise wrong. The old async generator awaited the value, so it was always spec-compliant. Wrap the result, e.g. `new Promise((resolve, reject) => then.call(chunk, ...))`, or use the `pump` path used for the slow case.

findings.title: Possible TypeError
findings.body:
The first condition uses optional chaining (`previous?.isCJ || next?.isCJ`), so either `previous` or `next` can be undefined. The second condition then reads `previous.kind` and `next.kind` without optional chaining.

This crashes when a whitespace node sits at the start or end of a sentence next to a CJ word. Example: a text node ending in `日本語\n` followed by an inline node such as emphasis or a link. Here `previous.isCJ` is true and `next` is undefined, so `next.kind` throws.

Use `previous?.kind` and `next?.kind`, or return early when either neighbor is missing.

If a whitespace node sits at the start or end of a sentence next to a CJ character, this throws a `TypeError`. Use optional chaining here too.

Improved code:
!(
  (previous?.kind === KIND_K_LETTER && next?.kind === KIND_CJ_LETTER) ||

)

findings.title: Possible crash
findings.body:
`previous` and `next` are only guarded with `?.` in the `isCJ` check. The negated clause then reads `previous.kind` and `next.kind` directly. A whitespace node can be the first or last child of a sentence, for example the trailing `\n` in a text node that ends right before an inline node.

Example: `日本語\n*強調*`. Here `previous.isCJ` is true and `next` is `undefined`. The first disjunct short-circuits, because `previous.kind` is not `KIND_K_LETTER`. findings.title: Stale dispatcher returned
findings.body:
Updates are silently lost if `globalThis` is frozen after the global dispatcher symbol already exists.

This happens in the common case: undici, or Node's bundled fetch, sets the dispatcher first, and the app calls `Object.freeze(globalThis)` later. Freezing makes the existing property non-writable, so a later `setGlobalDispatcher(newAgent)` fails in `defineProperty`. The `TypeError` is caught and `newAgent` goes into `fallbackDispatcher`.

However, `getGlobalDispatcher` returns `globalThis[globalDispatcher] ?? fallbackDispatcher`. The global property is still the old agent, so the fallback is never read. The call appears to succeed but has no effect, and requests keep using the old agent.

Fix options:
- Have `getGlobalDispatcher` prefer `fallbackDispatcher` once it is set.
- Or clear `fallbackDispatcher` on a successful define and check it first.

findings.title: Silent stale session
findings.body: `cached_db` reads from the cache before the database. If the cache delete fails, the DB row is gone but the cached session data stays valid until the cache entry expires. Before this change, the exception made `delete()` and `flush()` (used by `logout()`) fail visibly. Now logout looks successful while a copy of the session cookie can still authenticate until cache expiry. Swallowing errors is fine for `save()`, but for `delete()` it is a security trade-off. Consider documenting this explicitly, or retrying or invalidating the entry another way (e.g. setting a short-lived tombstone).

findings.title: Stale session survives delete
findings.body:
Before this change, a failed cache delete raised an exception, so callers saw that invalidation had failed. Now the error is only logged, and the delete appears to succeed. The DB row is gone, but the cached entry remains. `cached_db`'s `load()` reads the cache first, so the "deleted" session keeps working until the cache entry expires.

This affects `flush()`, which is used by `logout()`. If the cache delete fails during logout, anyone who still holds the old session cookie (for example, a stolen one) stays authenticated. Swallowing write failures is mostly harmless because reads fall back to the DB, but delete failures directly undermine session invalidation.

Consider at least documenting this risk explicitly. If silently keeping a valid session is not intended, reconsider swallowing the error. This trade-off probably also deserves wider discussion.

findings.title: Breaks async views
findings.body:
The new `wrapper` is always a plain sync function. When `non_atomic_requests` decorates an `async def` view, `iscoroutinefunction(wrapper)` returns False. Django's handler then treats the view as sync. It calls the view in a thread and gets back an un-awaited coroutine instead of an `HttpResponse`, so the request fails ("didn't return an HttpResponse object").

This is a regression, because the previous implementation returned the original view unchanged. When `iscoroutinefunction(view)` is true, the decorator should define an `async def` wrapper that awaits the view. Alternatively, it can mark the wrapper with `markcoroutinefunction`. Adding a test with an async view would catch this.

findings.title: Closing-tag regression
findings.body:
`_comment_end_re` and `_verbatim_end_re` use `[^\S\n]+`, which requires at least one whitespace character after `{%`. The old lexer compared the stripped tag content, so `{% verbatim %}x{%endverbatim%}` and `{% comment %}x{%endcomment%}` both worked.

With this change, the raw-aware splitter never finds the closing tag. The rest of the template becomes a single text token, and the parser raises an "unclosed tag" `TemplateSyntaxError`.

The behavior is also inconsistent within the PR. The opening tag is detected after `strip()`, so `{%verbatim%}` and `{%comment%}` open a raw block. The named-verbatim end regex uses `[^\S\n]*`, so it accepts `{%endverbatim name%}`. Using `*` instead of `+` in these two regexes would restore the old behavior.
findings.label: defect:d1

findings.title: Inconsistent raw detection
findings.body:
`_raw_start_re` requires whitespace after `{%` (`\s+`), but `_raw_end_tag_re` strips the content and also treats `{%comment%}` and `{%verbatim%}` as raw openers. As a result, the same template tokenizes differently depending on whether some other `{% comment ...` or `{% verbatim ...` with a space appears elsewhere.

Example: `{%comment%}{{ x }}{%endcomment%}` works on the fast path when it is the only raw tag. If the template also contains `{% verbatim %}...{% endverbatim %}`, it goes through `_tag_re_split` instead. There the `{%comment%}` block enters raw mode and cannot be closed, because of the whitespace requirement in the end regex.

The fast-path check should accept optional whitespace (`\s*`) so it matches what `_raw_end_tag_re` accepts.
findings.label: defect:d1

findings.title: Allow closing tags without inner whitespace
findings.body:
The closing-tag regexes require at least one space after `{%`, so `{%endcomment%}` and `{%endverbatim%}` no longer close their blocks. Both were valid before, because the content is stripped and compared. Without a match, the rest of the template is swallowed as text and parsing fails with an unclosed-tag error. Use `*` instead of `+`, matching the named-verbatim regex.

Improved code:
_comment_end_re = re.compile(
    r"%s[^\S\n]*endcomment[^\S\n]*%s"
    % (re.escape(BLOCK_TAG_START), re.escape(BLOCK_TAG_END))
)
_verbatim_end_re = re.compile(
    r"%s[^\S\n]*endverbatim[^\S\n]*%s"
    % (re.escape(BLOCK_TAG_START), re.escape(BLOCK_TAG_END))
)
findings.label: defect:d1

findings.title: Detect raw opening tags without whitespace
findings.body:
The fast-path detector requires whitespace after `{%`, so a template using `{%verbatim%}` takes the plain `tag_re.split` path. The verbatim handling was removed from `create_token`, so the verbatim content would then be tokenized and rendered as template syntax. This is a regression. Make the whitespace optional so that every opening tag recognized by `_raw_end_tag_re` (which strips the content) triggers the raw-aware splitter.

Improved code:
_raw_start_re = re.compile(
    r"%s\s*(?:comment|verbatim)\b" % re.escape(BLOCK_TAG_START)
)
findings.label: defect:d1

findings.title: Closing tag regression
findings.body:
`_comment_end_re` and `_verbatim_end_re` require at least one whitespace character after `{%` (`[^\S\n]+`). The old lexer compared stripped content, so tags without spaces closed the block.

Now the lexer looks only for the closing tag inside a raw block. When the closing tag has no spaces, it never matches and the rest of the template becomes text.
- `{% comment %}x{%endcomment%}` now fails with an unclosed `comment` tag error.
- `{% verbatim %}x{%endverbatim%}` now fails with an unclosed `verbatim` tag error.

Both used to work. The named-verbatim regex uses `[^\S\n]*`, which is inconsistent with these two. Allow optional whitespace (`*`) in the fixed regexes too, and add tests for the no-space forms.
findings.label: defect:d1

findings.title: Verbatim without spaces
findings.body:
`_raw_start_re` requires whitespace after `{%` (`\s+`). The verbatim handling was also removed from `create_token`. As a result, a template like `{%verbatim%}{{ x }}{%endverbatim%}` takes the fast `tag_re.split` path, and the inner content is tokenized as real tags.

The `verbatim` tag renders its nodelist with an empty `Context`, so the output becomes `""` instead of the literal `{{ x }}`. This is a silent output change. Previously `content[:9] == "verbatim"` handled this case.

The behavior also depends on unrelated content. If another raw tag with spaces appears anywhere in the template, the slow path runs and `{%verbatim%}` is treated as raw.

Use `\s*` in `_raw_start_re`, which still works because false positives are filtered by `_raw_end_tag_re`.
findings.label: defect:d1

findings.title: Detect raw blocks without leading whitespace
findings.body:
The fast-path check requires whitespace after `{%`. A template like `{%verbatim%}{{ x }}{%endverbatim%}` therefore never matches and goes through plain `tag_re.split()`. Since `create_token()` no longer tracks verbatim state, the inner `{{ x }}` becomes a `VAR` token and renders as a variable instead of literal text. The old lexer handled this case because it stripped the tag content, so this is a regression. Allow zero or more whitespace characters, which matches how `_raw_end_tag_re()` strips the content.

Improved code:
_raw_start_re = re.compile(
    r"%s\s*(?:comment|verbatim)\b" % re.escape(BLOCK_TAG_START)
)

findings.body:
The new regexes require at least one whitespace character after `{%`. `_raw_start_re` uses `\s+`, and `_comment_end_re` and `_verbatim_end_re` use `[^\S\n]+`. Django has always accepted block tags without inner whitespace, such as `{%verbatim%}` and `{%endcomment%}`, because the content is stripped. Two cases now break:

findings.title: Duplicate kwarg
findings.body:
`sort_keys=False` is passed explicitly, and `**self.options` is also passed. If a caller passes `sort_keys` to the serializer, the call raises `TypeError: got multiple values for keyword argument 'sort_keys'`. Example: `serializers.serialize("yaml", qs, sort_keys=True)`.

Before this change, that option was forwarded to `yaml.dump` without error. It had no effect because of the dict representer, but it did not crash.

Use `self.options.setdefault("sort_keys", False)`, as is already done for `allow_unicode`. This keeps the default and also lets callers override it.
findings.label: defect:d1

findings.title: Avoid duplicate keyword argument TypeError
findings.body:
Passing `sort_keys=False` explicitly alongside `**self.options` raises `TypeError: got multiple values for keyword argument 'sort_keys'` whenever a caller supplies `sort_keys` to `serializers.serialize("yaml", ...)`. Before this change, that option was simply forwarded to `yaml.dump`, so this is a regression. Set the default with `setdefault`, as `allow_unicode` already does, so caller-supplied values are still honored.

Improved code:
def end_serialization(self):
    self.options.setdefault("allow_unicode", True)
    self.options.setdefault("sort_keys", False)
    yaml.dump(
        self.objects,
        self.stream,
        Dumper=DjangoSafeDumper,
        **self.options,
    )

findings.title: Avoid unconditional plain-array output allocation
findings.body:
The array branch always writes into a freshly allocated plain `np.zeros` buffer, even when no endpoints are equal. This silently drops array subclasses and their extra state, such as masks or units, that the original `np.subtract(stop, start, ...)` preserved, so `linspace` can behave differently for subclass inputs. Use the original subtraction unless some elements are actually equal, and use the `where=` path only in that case.

Improved code:
equal = start == stop
if equal.ndim == 0:
    delta = dt.type(0) if equal else np.subtract(
        stop, start, dtype=type(dt))
elif not equal.any():
    delta = np.subtract(stop, start, dtype=type(dt))
else:
    delta = np.subtract(stop, start, dtype=type(dt), where=~equal,
                        out=np.zeros(equal.shape, dtype=type(dt)))

findings.title: Use thread-safe errstate instead of warnings filter
findings.body:
CI runs the suite under `pytest-run-parallel`. `warnings.catch_warnings()` with `simplefilter` changes process-global warning state, so it is not thread-safe and can make this test, or tests running beside it, fail intermittently. `np.errstate` is context-local, so `np.errstate(invalid="raise")` is safe there and checks the exact floating-point "invalid value" condition the fix targets. Make the same change to the `with warnings.catch_warnings():` line and drop the now-unused `import warnings`.

Improved code:
with np.errstate(invalid="raise"):
    for inf in [np.inf, -np.inf]:

findings.title: Subclass Regression
findings.body: For N-d inputs, `delta` is now written into a plain `np.zeros(...)` ndarray passed as `out=`. Previously `np.subtract(stop, start, ...)` allocated its own output and could return an `ndarray` subclass (e.g. a unit-carrying or masked array) via `__array_wrap__`/`__array_ufunc__`. Passing a base-class `out` can drop that subclass type, units or mask from `delta`, and so from the `linspace` result for array-valued endpoints. The scalar branch has no such issue. It is uncertain whether any supported subclass is affected, since the diff does not show how `start`/`stop` are converted. A subclass test, or building `out` with `np.zeros_like`/`empty_like`-style subclass preservation, would settle it.

findings.title: Avoid cast
findings.body:
`cast("DataFrame", selected_obj)` is added only to narrow the type after an `ndim == 2` check. The project's typing guidelines say `typing.cast` is "strongly discouraged".

Narrowing with an `isinstance` check gives the type checker the same information without the cast, for example:

```python
if isinstance(selected_obj, ABCDataFrame):
    return selected_obj._constructor(...)
```

`ABCDataFrame` is already used in this function.

When no argument resolves to an existing path, the fallback now loads only `invocation_dir`. The old `_try_load_conftest(invocation_dir, ...)` also scanned its `test*` subdirectories. Fix: apply the `test*` subdirectory expansion to the fallback anchor too. For example, build the anchor list first, then expand each anchor with its `test*` subdirectories.

findings.body:
The checks use `last_op_result().is_none()` on `fetch_build_data_queue` and `fetch_proc_macros_queue`. That is true only while the op has never completed, which contradicts the comment ("have finished fetching the build data once" / "finished loading the proc-macros once").

The comment says to fetch semantic diagnostics only after build data and proc-macros have finished loading once. The checks use `last_op_result().is_none() && !op_in_progress()`, which is true only when the op has never run or been queued.

This has two effects:

- Once each queue completes and `last_op_result` becomes `Some`, `fetch_semantic` stays `false`. Semantic diagnostics are then never published again when `run_build_scripts` or `expand_proc_macros` is enabled, which is the default.

This should likely be `last_op_result().is_some()`. It may also need `!op_in_progress()`, depending on whether reruns should suppress diagnostics.

findings.title: Comma Path Splitting
findings.body:
The server splits the `paths` value on `,`, but commas are valid, unencoded characters in URL pathnames. `location.pathname` keeps commas as-is, for example `/tags/a,b` or `/products/1,2`. On the client, `paths.join(",")` turns `/tags/a,b` into the same string as the two paths `/tags/a` and `b`. The server then requests patches for the wrong paths, so the route is never discovered and the navigation 404s.

Previously, repeated `p` params handled these paths correctly. To fix this, encode each path before joining (for example with `encodeURIComponent`) and decode each entry after splitting. Alternatively, use a delimiter that cannot appear in a pathname.

For slots, the old code used a close marker found by walking from the open marker. The new code uses `locateClaimedEnd`, which trusts the cursor whenever nothing is cached. While the slot boundary is still hydrating, the cursor may rest on a nested `]` close, so the wrong anchor can be reused. Use `locateSlotEndAnchor()` for slots, matching its documented contract of never reading off the cursor.

Improved code:
const close =
  frag.__vf & SLOT
    ? locateSlotEndAnchor()
    : frag.hydrationClaim && frag.hydrationClaim.start
      ? locateClaimedEnd(frag.hydrationClaim.start)
      : null
findings.label: valid

findings.title: Unneeded walk (nit)
findings.body:
This call runs after `scope.run(render)`, so the slot content has already hydrated. Even so, `locateSlotEndAnchor()` always walks from the open marker via `locateEndAnchor`.

By the docs in this PR, the cursor normally rests on the close at this point. `locateClaimedEnd` would usually return it without walking. Using `locateSlotEndAnchor()` here keeps the eager-walk cost the PR is trying to remove, at least on the `!currentParentNode` path.

Suggested fix: expose a variant built on `locateClaimedEnd(claim.start)` for post-content callers. Keep the walking version for the in-progress case in `prepareDeferredHydrationAnchor`.
findings.label: invalid

findings.title: Restore the null guard before trimming
findings.body:
The old code only trimmed when a close marker was found (`if (close) trimHydrationBoundary(close)`). The new code calls `trimHydrationBoundary` unconditionally, so it can receive `null` when there is no `claim.start` or the close cannot be located. Depending on how `trimHydrationBoundary` handles `null`, this can trim the wrong nodes or throw. Keep the guard so the change stays behavior-preserving.

Improved code:
const close = claim.start ? locateClaimedEnd(claim.start) : null
if (close) trimHydrationBoundary(close)

findings.title: Possible Bug
findings.body: For slot fragments, `planReuseOwnClose` now calls `locateClaimedEnd(claim.start)`. When the close has not been cached in `$fe`, that function checks the cursor first and returns it if it is a matching close comment. The new `locateSlotEndAnchor` doc comment says the close must be located by walking from the open marker, "never read off the cursor", because slot content may still be under way. The old code used the eagerly located `currentSlotEndAnchor`. If this runs mid-hydration while the cursor rests on a nested or enclosing `]` close, the slot can reuse the wrong anchor. Use `locateSlotEndAnchor()` (walk-based) for the SLOT case to match the other call sites. I could not see the rest of `locateClaimedEnd` to confirm whether it validates the cursor node further.

findings.title: Possible Bug
findings.body: `planReuseOwnClose` now resolves a slot's close with `locateClaimedEnd(claim.start)`, which first checks the cursor. The old code used the eagerly located close, and the new `locateSlotEndAnchor` doc comment says the close must be walked to from the open marker and "never read off the cursor". If this path runs while the slot content is still hydrating, or after a nested range of the same kind (`)` or `]`) has been consumed, the cursor can rest on a nested or enclosing close. That close would then be returned and cached in `$fe` as the slot's end, so the anchor is wrong. This should be confirmed: either `planReuseOwnClose` is only reached once the content is fully hydrated, or it should use `locateEndAnchor` like `locateSlotEndAnchor` does. A test would help, such as a slot containing a nested fragment with an unresolved deferred branch.

findings.title: Avoid cursor-based end lookup in finally
findings.body:
`locateClaimedEnd` now returns `start.$fe` only if it was already cached; otherwise it still reads the cursor, which can rest on an enclosing close marker of the same kind after the slot content was claimed. Resolving through `locateEndAnchor(claim.start)`, as `locateSlotEndAnchor` does, avoids trimming the wrong boundary. A direct walk is more reliable in the `finally` block, including when `fn()` throws midway.

Improved code:
trimHydrationBoundary(claim.start ? locateEndAnchor(claim.start) : null)
findings.label: valid
